ezra-4:1:6.summary: Uses “sons of the deported community” in a later, unrelated inquiry.

ezra-4:1:7.summary: Solomon had “no plotter” as he resolved to build the Lord’s house, unlike the returnees who face oppressors.

ezra-4:1:10.summary: Sanaballat “heard that we were building the wall” and opposed it, closely paralleling enemies hearing of the temple building (truncated range).

ezra-4:1:12.summary: Shares the phrase “sons of the deportation”, here keeping Passover after the temple’s completion.

ezra-4:2:1.summary: Asordan’s accession after Sennacherib identifies the Assyrian king Asaraddon who settled these people.

ezra-4:2:2.summary: False brothers slipping in to spy is loosely like outsiders offering to join the work with ulterior motives.

ezra-4:2:6.summary: Workers disguising themselves as servants of righteousness loosely parallels enemies posing as fellow worshippers.

ezra-4:2:9.summary: Speaking wickedness against the height has no specific link to the outsiders’ offer to build.

ezra-4:2:10.summary: False teachers who “secretly bring in” factions loosely parallel adversaries seeking entry into the work.

ezra-4:2:11.summary: Jannes and Jambres openly opposing Moses does not match a friendly-sounding offer to help build.

ezra-4:2:12.summary: Mentions the same “leaders of the families” at the foundation-laying, the preceding scene.

ezra-4:2:13.summary: Hosea’s “Assur will certainly not save us” shares only the name of Assyria.

ezra-4:2:14.summary: Ezra 2:2 lists those who came with Zorobabel, the leader approached in the source.

ezra-4:2:15.summary: Zorobabel and his brothers built the altar and offered sacrifices, the worship the outsiders claim to share.

ezra-4:2:16.summary: An enemy who agrees with his lips but devises deceits fits the adversaries’ friendly offer only in general terms.

ezra-4:3:0.summary: Nehemiah tells opponents “we will build” and they have “no share” in Jerusalem, closely matching the refusal of partnership.

ezra-4:3:9.summary: The text of Cyrus’s decision to build God’s house in Jerusalem, the command Zorobabel cites.

ezra-4:5:0.summary: A “scheme, devising evil things” against the Lord loosely fits the counsel hired against the builders.

ezra-4:5:3.summary: Rulers gathering against the Lord is a general parallel to plans against the builders.

ezra-4:15:8.summary: Sedekias “broke faith” with Babylon’s king and Jerusalem was besieged, the rebellion and ruin the letter recalls.

ezra-4:19:6.summary: Ezekiel describes Judah’s king revolting against Babylon’s king, a revolt behind “risen against kings” (truncated range).

ezra-6:14:4.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

ezra-6:14:5.summary: Zacharias’s vision of measuring and repopulating Jerusalem broadly relates to his prophecy supporting the rebuilding.

ezra-6:14:6.summary: Isaiah says Cyrus will do God’s wishes and the holy house will be rebuilt, fulfilled in the decree of Cyrus.

ezra-6:14:8.summary: The leaders build the house “as Cyrus king of the Persians commanded,” the same royal decree basis.
ezra-6:14:8.why: Shows the builders relying on Cyrus’s order.

ezra-6:14:9.summary: Haggai’s command to “rebuild the house” is the prophecy of Haggai through which the elders built.
ezra-6:14:9.why: Gives the content of Haggai’s prophecy.

ezra-6:14:10.summary: The Levites set over the work in the Lord’s house began the building that Ezra 6:14 reports completed.
ezra-6:14:10.why: Shows the start of the rebuilding.

ezra-6:14:11.summary: Zechariah’s promise that Zerubbabel’s hands will complete this house is the prophecy behind the completed rebuilding.
ezra-6:14:11.why: Prophecy fulfilled in completing the temple.

ezra-6:14:12.summary: Haggai urges Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people to work on the house, the prophecy through which they built (shown text truncated).
ezra-6:14:12.why: Shows the prophetic encouragement to build.

ezra-6:14:13.summary: Zechariah’s vision of chariots (truncated, later about building the temple) relates only loosely in the shown text.

ezra-6:15:0.summary: Both mention the month of “Adar,” but Esther concerns Haman’s lot, not the temple’s completion.

ezra-6:15:1.summary: Esther’s festival days in “Adar” share only the month name with the temple’s completion date.

ezra-6:15:2.summary: Esther dates an event to “Adar,” sharing only the month with the temple’s completion.

ezra-6:15:3.summary: Rest on the fourteenth of the month shares no specific element; Adar is not even named in this verse.

ezra-6:15:4.summary: Purim observance in “Adar” shares only the month name with the temple’s completion date.

ezra-6:15:5.summary: Haman’s letters target the month “Adar,” sharing only the month with Ezra 6:15.

ezra-6:15:6.summary: Esther 9:1 names the thirteenth of “Adar,” sharing only the month with Ezra 6:15.

ezra-6:15:7.summary: The Jews in Susa act on the fourteenth of “Adar,” sharing only the month name.

ezra-6:15:8.summary: Sirach recalls that in Joshua son of Jozadak’s days “they built a house” for the Lord, the temple completed here.
ezra-6:15:8.why: Later praise of the second temple’s builders.

ezra-6:16:17.summary: The Maccabees “celebrated the dedication” of the altar with gladness, paralleling the joyful dedication of God’s house.

ezra-6:16:0.summary: Solomon and the people “dedicated God’s house,” the first temple’s dedication paralleling the second.

ezra-6:16:2.summary: Paul’s general exhortation to rejoice shares only the word joy with the temple dedication.

ezra-6:16:3.summary: The feast of Dedication in Jerusalem relates to temple dedication, though it commemorates the Maccabean, not this, dedication.
ezra-6:16:3.why: Links to later temple dedication festival.

ezra-6:16:4.summary: The same returned community keeps the following festival “with joy” in connection with the house of God.
ezra-6:16:4.why: Continues the joyful celebrations of the restored temple.

ezra-6:16:5.summary: Rejoicing at going to the Lord’s house broadly matches joy over the house’s dedication.
ezra-6:16:5.why: Devotional echo of joy in God’s house.

ezra-6:16:6.summary: Great rejoicing in Jerusalem at Hezekiah’s festival broadly parallels the joyful dedication.

ezra-6:16:7.summary: The list of Israel, “the priests, the Levites” resembles the groups named, but in a settlement context.

ezra-6:16:8.summary: The joyful founding of the Lord’s house by priests, Levites and people precedes this joyful dedication.
ezra-6:16:8.why: Links founding and dedication of the temple.

ezra-6:16:9.summary: The “sons of the deportation” building the Lord’s house are the same community dedicating it.

ezra-6:16:10.summary: Hezekiah’s assembly keeping days “with rejoicing” broadly parallels joyful temple celebration.

ezra-6:16:11.summary: All Israel bringing up the ark with music loosely parallels a joyful sacred celebration.

ezra-6:16:12.summary: Rejoicing before the Lord at the chosen place broadly fits the joyful dedication.

ezra-6:16:13.summary: Priests, Levites and the sons of Israel are listed, a loose overlap of the community’s groups.

ezra-6:16:14.summary: Solomon’s altar dedication feast ends with the people rejoicing, paralleling the joyful dedication of the second temple.
ezra-6:16:14.why: Compares first and second temple dedications.

ezra-6:16:15.summary: The wall dedication with great sacrifices and gladness parallels the temple dedication celebrated with joy.
ezra-6:16:15.why: Later joyful dedication in restored Jerusalem.

ezra-6:16:16.summary: Nehemiah urges festive joy on a holy day, broadly like joy at the dedication.
ezra-6:16:16.why: Shows joy as fitting for holy days.

ezra-6:16:18.summary: The yearly celebration of the altar’s dedication “with gladness and joy” parallels the joyful temple dedication.

ezra-6:17:0.summary: Returned exiles offer bulls, rams, lambs and “twelve male goats for sin” for all Israel, the same pattern.
ezra-6:17:0.why: Shows the same twelve-tribe sin offering.

ezra-6:17:10.summary: Elijah takes twelve stones “according to the number of Israel’s tribes,” the same phrase used for the twelve goats.
ezra-6:17:10.why: Shows symbolic representation of all twelve tribes.

ezra-6:17:1.summary: Hezekiah offers calves, rams, lambs and “male goats for sin” for Israel at the temple’s rededication.

ezra-6:17:2.summary: Revelation’s sealed of every tribe of Israel shares the twelve-tribe idea only (shown text truncated).
ezra-6:17:2.why: Twelve tribes as symbol of all Israel.

ezra-6:17:3.summary: Solomon’s huge offering when the people “dedicated God’s house” contrasts with the modest offering of the second dedication.
ezra-6:17:3.why: Compares scale of the two dedications.

ezra-6:17:4.summary: Hezekiah’s numbered calves, rams and lambs at the temple’s restoration parallel the listed dedication offerings.

ezra-6:17:6.summary: The congregation’s sin offering law loosely underlies an offering “for sin on behalf of all Israel,” though with a calf.
ezra-6:17:6.why: Legal background for communal sin offering.

ezra-6:17:7.summary: Solomon’s great sacrifice as “the king and all the sons of Israel dedicated the Lord’s house” parallels this dedication.

ezra-6:17:8.summary: Burnt offerings when the ark was installed broadly parallel sacrifices for a sacred dedication.

ezra-6:17:9.summary: Law of a sin offering for the high priest’s sin is only general background to the goats for sin.

ezra-6:17:11.summary: A female goat for sin shares only the general sin-offering background with the male goats offered.

ezra-6:17:12.summary: An unblemished “male young goat” for sin parallels the male goats for sin, as general legal background.
ezra-6:17:12.why: Legal basis for male goat sin offerings.

ezra-6:17:13.summary: The “twelve tribes of Israel” appear in both, but Luke’s context of judging thrones is unrelated.
ezra-6:17:13.why: Shows twelve tribes as all Israel.

ezra-6:17:14.summary: The twelve tribes named on the heavenly city’s gates share only the twelve-tribe symbolism.
ezra-6:17:14.why: Twelve tribes as symbol of all Israel.

ezra-6:18:1.summary: Josiah arranges priests and Levites by courses and “divisions” for service “according to the writing,” matching Ezra’s organization.

ezra-6:18:2.summary: The “divisions” of Aaron’s sons are the priestly courses in which the priests were stationed.

ezra-6:18:3.summary: Moses’ law appointing the Levites to the Lord’s works is part of the “book of Moses” basis for their service (shown text truncated).

ezra-6:18:4.summary: David divides the Levites into service courses, background to stationing them in groups for the temple service (truncated).

ezra-6:19:2.summary: Israel “kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month,” a close verbal parallel at another new beginning.
ezra-6:19:2.why: Parallel Passover at a new start.

ezra-6:19:0.summary: The original Passover law sets the lamb for “the fourteenth day of this month,” the date the returnees kept (shown text truncated).
ezra-6:19:0.why: Mosaic institution of the Passover date.

ezra-6:19:1.summary: Hezekiah’s great Passover in Jerusalem after the temple’s cleansing parallels the returnees’ Passover after dedication (shown text truncated).

ezra-6:20:0.summary: At Josiah’s Passover priests and Levites “sacrificed the Passover,” paralleling the Levites slaughtering it here.
ezra-6:20:0.why: Shows Levites’ role in Passover slaughter.

ezra-6:20:1.summary: Priests offering for themselves and the people loosely parallels slaughtering for their brothers and themselves.

ezra-6:20:2.summary: Hezekiah’s Levites purified themselves and assisted the priests, paralleling the purified priests and Levites slaughtering the Passover.

ezra-6:20:4.summary: Moses commands to “slaughter the Passover,” the original instruction behind the act described.

ezra-6:21:0.summary: The land filled with the peoples’ “uncleanness” is what those joining Israel separated from.
ezra-6:21:0.why: Explains the uncleanness of the nations.

ezra-6:21:1.summary: Isaiah’s call to “separate yourselves” from the unclean broadly matches separating from the nations’ uncleanness.

ezra-6:21:2.summary: Cleansing from every defilement broadly parallels separating from the nations’ uncleanness.

ezra-6:21:3.summary: Later the people “have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands,” contrasting with this separation.
ezra-6:21:3.why: Shows later failure to remain separated.

ezra-6:21:5.summary: The sons of Israel “separated themselves” from foreigners, a similar act of separation by the restored community.

ezra-6:21:6.summary: God cleansing Israel from uncleanness broadly relates to separating from the nations’ uncleanness.

ezra-6:21:7.summary: Passover rules for the unclean relate loosely to purity for eating the Passover (shown text truncated).

ezra-6:21:8.summary: Sanctity befitting God’s house is only a general purity theme, with no specific link to the Passover meal.

ezra-6:21:9.summary: Men unclean and unable to keep the Passover shares the purity-for-Passover concern only loosely.

ezra-6:21:10.summary: Those “coming from the peoples of the land to the law of God” parallel those separating to seek the Lord.
ezra-6:21:10.why: Shows outsiders joining the covenant community.

ezra-6:21:11.summary: “Be separated … do not touch anything unclean” broadly echoes separating from the nations’ uncleanness.

ezra-6:22:1.summary: Israel keeps “the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great rejoicing,” closely matching Ezra’s wording.

ezra-6:22:2.summary: The Lord stirring Cyrus’s spirit parallels the Lord turning the king’s heart toward the Jews.

ezra-6:22:3.summary: Josiah’s people keep the Passover and “the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days,” the same sequence.

ezra-6:22:4.summary: God put it “in the king’s heart” to glorify the Lord’s house, the same idea as turning the king’s heart.
ezra-6:22:4.why: Repeated theme of God moving kings.

ezra-6:22:5.summary: The Greek Proverbs 16:7 on righteous deeds over sacrifices does not carry the assumed link about enemies at peace.
ezra-6:22:5.why: Septuagint wording removes the intended link.

ezra-6:22:6.summary: The law commands eating unleavened bread “for seven days,” the basis for the festival kept here.

ezra-6:22:7.summary: Authority given from above loosely relates to God turning a ruler’s heart.
ezra-6:22:7.why: Theology of divine control over rulers.

ezra-6:22:8.summary: “For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread” is the law behind the seven-day festival.

ezra-6:22:9.summary: The “first day of Unleavened Bread” links to the same festival but in Jesus’ era.

ezra-6:22:10.summary: A “king of the Assyrians” is named, but the unusual title for the Persian king is the only link.
ezra-6:22:10.why: Context for the Assyrian royal title.

ezra-6:22:11.summary: Paul’s call to keep the feast with unleavened bread spiritualizes the festival observed here.

ezra-6:22:12.summary: Return from the Assyrians loosely relates to the “king of Assour” favoring the returned Jews.
ezra-6:22:12.why: Context for Assyria in restoration hopes.

ezra-6:22:13.summary: The “king of Assyria’s” forces taking Manasseh to Babylon share only the Assyrian royal title.

ezra-6:22:14.summary: Darius’s decree funding and protecting the work shows how the king’s heart was turned to strengthen the work (shown text truncated).
ezra-6:22:14.why: Concrete evidence of the king’s favor.

ezra-7:1:15.summary: The family leaders who came up with Esdras “in the reign of Arthasastha” belong to the same journey.

ezra-7:1:0.summary: Nehemiah serves the same King Arthasastha, placing both missions in his reign.
ezra-7:1:0.why: Same Persian king for both reformers.

ezra-7:1:2.summary: Arthasastha, king of the Persians, is named among the kings whose decrees supported the house.

ezra-7:1:3.summary: Arthasastha decrees support for “Esdras the priest and scribe,” the same king and Esdras.
ezra-7:1:3.why: Shows the king’s support for Esdras.

ezra-7:1:4.summary: Chelkias the high priest may be the “Elkia” of Esdras’s genealogy, though spellings differ and the link is not explicit.

ezra-7:1:5.summary: Arthasastha’s letter is addressed “to Esdras, scribe of the law,” the same king and Esdras.

ezra-7:1:6.summary: Chelkias finding the book of the law may be Esdras’s ancestor Elkia, but the shown texts do not confirm it.

ezra-7:1:7.summary: “Esdras the priest” reads the law to the assembly, the same Esdras introduced here (shown text truncated).

ezra-7:1:8.summary: “Azaria son of Chelkia” matches the genealogy’s “Azarias, son of Elkia” in the high-priestly line.

ezra-7:1:9.summary: Hilkiah the high priest may be the Elkia of Esdras’s line, but the spelling differs in the Saints text.

ezra-7:1:10.summary: The chief priest taken to Babylon is unnamed in the Saints text shown, so the link to Saraias is implicit.

ezra-7:1:11.summary: Esdras had set his heart to seek and teach the law, describing the same Esdras introduced here.

ezra-7:1:12.summary: “Saraia son of Elkia” in the priestly genealogy matches Esdras’s ancestors Saraias and Elkia.

ezra-7:1:13.summary: “Saraias the first priest” taken captive is Esdras’s named ancestor Saraias.

ezra-7:1:14.summary: Hilkiah finding the book of the law may be Esdras’s ancestor Elkia, though the Saints spelling differs.

ezra-7:2:0.summary: Zadok appointed first priest by Solomon is the “Saddouk” in Esdras’s genealogy, despite spelling differences.

ezra-7:2:1.summary: “Zadok son of Ahitub” matches the genealogy’s “Saddouk, son of Achitob.”

ezra-7:5:21.summary: Aaron’s sons Eleazar, Phinees and Abisou give the same high-priestly descent as Esdras’s genealogy.

ezra-7:5:0.summary: “Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest” names the same ancestors in Esdras’s line.
ezra-7:5:0.why: Shows Phinehas’s zeal in Esdras’s ancestry.

ezra-7:5:1.summary: “Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the high priest” matches the same ancestral chain.

ezra-7:5:2.summary: Aaron and his son Eleazar, who succeeds him, are the ancestors named in Esdras’s line.

ezra-7:5:3.summary: Eleazar the priest appears, but the verse adds nothing about the genealogy.
ezra-7:5:3.why: Mentions an ancestor only in passing.

ezra-7:5:5.summary: An unnamed chief priest rebuking Uzziah has no specific link to Esdras’s genealogy.
ezra-7:5:5.why: Only the generic title of chief priest.

ezra-7:5:6.summary: “Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest” names the same ancestors.

ezra-7:5:7.summary: “Eleazar son of Aaron the priest” is the ancestor named in Esdras’s line.

ezra-7:5:8.summary: Aaron called by God to priesthood relates to Aaron “the first priest” only generally.

ezra-7:5:9.summary: Phinehas’s atonement reckoned as righteousness recalls the same Phinees in Esdras’s genealogy.

ezra-7:5:10.summary: Eleazar the priest appears, but the verse adds little beyond the name.
ezra-7:5:10.why: Mentions an ancestor only in passing.

ezra-7:5:11.summary: Eleazar son of Aaron fathers Phinehas, the same descent named in Esdras’s genealogy.

ezra-7:5:12.summary: Eleazar the priest appears in the land allotment, sharing only the ancestor’s name.
ezra-7:5:12.why: Mentions an ancestor only in passing.

ezra-7:5:13.summary: Eleazar, Aaron’s son, heads the priestly line through which Sadok descends, as in Esdras’s genealogy (shown text truncated).

ezra-7:5:14.summary: Amarias the priest may be one of the Amariahs of the high-priestly line, but this verse is not genealogical.
ezra-7:5:14.why: Possible member of the priestly line.

ezra-7:5:15.summary: Eleazar the priest appears receiving gold, sharing only the ancestor’s name.
ezra-7:5:15.why: Mentions an ancestor only in passing.

ezra-7:5:16.summary: Phinehas the priest appears, but the episode adds little to the genealogy.
ezra-7:5:16.why: Mentions an ancestor only in passing.

ezra-7:5:17.summary: Aaron and his son Eleazar are named, sharing only the ancestors’ names.

ezra-7:5:18.summary: “Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron” repeats the same ancestral chain as Esdras’s genealogy.

ezra-7:5:19.summary: “Eleazar son of Aaron, the high priest” and Phinehas his son match the genealogy’s chain.

ezra-7:5:20.summary: Aaron and Eleazar are named in a sacrificial instruction, sharing only the ancestors’ names.

ezra-7:5:22.summary: Eleazar, son of Aaron, appears in an unrelated episode, sharing only the name.
ezra-7:5:22.why: Mentions an ancestor only in passing.

ezra-7:6:0.summary: Esdras speaks of “the hand of our God” upon those who seek Him, the same refrain as in 7:6.
ezra-7:6:0.why: Repeated theme of God’s guiding hand.

ezra-7:6:1.summary: Esdras credits royal favor to “the good hand of God” upon him, echoing 7:6.
ezra-7:6:1.why: Same refrain explaining the king’s favor.

ezra-7:6:2.summary: “The hand of our God was upon us” on the journey repeats the refrain of 7:6.
ezra-7:6:2.why: Shows God’s hand guiding the journey.

ezra-7:6:3.summary: Nehemiah likewise attributes the king’s words to “the hand of God, which was good upon me.”
ezra-7:6:3.why: Parallel favor from Arthasastha by God’s hand.

ezra-7:6:4.summary: “The king granted it to me, according to the good hand of God” closely matches Esdras’s royal favor.
ezra-7:6:4.why: Close parallel of royal grant and God’s hand.

ezra-7:6:5.summary: Christ’s promise to be with the disciples shares no specific element with Esdras’s royal favor.
ezra-7:6:5.why: Only a generic theme of divine presence.

ezra-7:6:6.summary: The king’s order to supply whatever “Esdras the priest and scribe of the law” asks shows the requests granted.
ezra-7:6:6.why: Details how the king granted his requests.

ezra-7:6:7.summary: Esdras came from Babylon “because the hand of his God was good upon him,” repeating 7:6.
ezra-7:6:7.why: Same refrain in the journey account.

ezra-7:6:8.summary: Arthasastha’s decree to Esdras, “scribe of the law,” is the grant of requests described in 7:6.

ezra-7:6:9.summary: Levites came “as the hand of our God was good upon us,” repeating Ezra’s refrain.
ezra-7:6:9.why: Same refrain of God’s good hand.

ezra-7:6:10.summary: The blessing for keeping commandments in Canaan has no specific link to Esdras the scribe’s journey.

ezra-7:6:11.summary: The Greek Proverbs 3:6 speaks of acknowledging wisdom, with no specific link to Esdras or God’s hand.

ezra-7:6:12.summary: Moses teaching “ordinances and judgments” relates loosely to Esdras as scribe in the law of Moses.
ezra-7:6:12.why: Background on the Mosaic law Esdras taught.

ezra-7:6:13.summary: Paul’s reminder of the gospel has no specific link to Esdras the scribe.

ezra-7:6:14.summary: A “swiftly writing scribe” echoes Esdras as a “ready scribe,” a verbal but not contextual link.
ezra-7:6:14.why: Image of a skilled, ready scribe.

ezra-7:6:15.summary: The Lord’s hand able to save loosely relates to the Lord’s hand upon Esdras.
ezra-7:6:15.why: General image of God’s powerful hand.

ezra-7:6:16.summary: Paul’s question “Where is the scribe?” shares only the word scribe with Esdras’s description.

ezra-7:6:17.summary: Paul’s instructions on pleasing God have no specific connection to Esdras or the king’s favor.

ezra-7:6:18.summary: A scribe trained for the kingdom bringing out treasures loosely relates to Esdras as a skilled scribe of the law.

ezra-7:6:19.summary: God’s hand strong enough to rescue loosely relates to the hand of God upon Esdras.
ezra-7:6:19.why: General image of God’s powerful hand.

ezra-7:6:20.summary: “Esdras the scribe” leads the wall-dedication procession, the same Esdras introduced here.

ezra-7:6:21.summary: Nehemiah prays for success and compassion before the king, broadly like Esdras receiving the king’s favor.

ezra-7:6:22.summary: Leaders gather around “Esdras the scribe” to study the law, showing the same scribe at work.

ezra-7:6:23.summary: God’s eyes upon Judah’s captivity loosely parallels God’s hand upon Esdras in royal dealings.
ezra-7:6:23.why: Theme of God watching over returnees.

ezra-7:6:24.summary: God scattering enemies’ counsel during wall-building has no specific link to Esdras’s favor with the king.

ezra-7:6:25.summary: God putting a plan into Nehemiah’s heart loosely parallels God’s guidance of Esdras.
ezra-7:6:25.why: Parallel divine prompting of a leader.

ezra-7:6:26.summary: The Lord turned the king’s heart toward them, the same divine influence behind the king granting Esdras’s requests.

ezra-7:6:27.summary: Jeremiah’s false pen of the scribes contrasts with Esdras as a faithful scribe of the law.

ezra-7:6:28.summary: “Esdras the priest and scribe” is named as active in Neemia’s days, the same person.

ezra-7:6:29.summary: Jacob’s renaming as Israel shares only the name Israel with Esdras’s description.

ezra-7:6:30.summary: “Esdras the scribe” stands on the platform to read the law, the same scribe in the law of Moses.
ezra-7:6:30.why: Shows Esdras reading the law publicly.

ezra-7:6:31.summary: “Esdras the priest and scribe” teaches the law with Neemias, the same person.

ezra-7:6:32.summary: Sirach on how a scribe gains wisdom relates generally to Esdras as a ready scribe.
ezra-7:6:32.why: Wisdom tradition on the scribe’s calling.

ezra-7:7:5.summary: The lists of gatekeepers, Nathinim and others name the same classes of returnees that went up (shown text truncated).
ezra-7:7:5.why: Shows the same groups among returnees.

ezra-7:7:0.summary: The family leaders who came up with Esdras under Arthasastha are the companions of this same journey (shown text truncated).
ezra-7:7:0.why: Lists the people in this return.

ezra-7:7:1.summary: “The priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, Nathinim” repeats the same list of community groups.

ezra-7:7:2.summary: David’s appointment of singers in the Lord’s house gives background for the singers who went up.

ezra-7:7:3.summary: David organizing Asaph’s and other singers provides background for the singers among the returnees.

ezra-7:7:4.summary: The decree exempts “priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, Nathinim” from tax, the same groups that went up.
ezra-7:7:4.why: Shows royal privileges for these groups.

ezra-7:7:6.summary: Nehemiah’s mission in the twentieth year of King Arthasastha places it thirteen years after this seventh-year journey.

ezra-7:7:7.summary: Arthasastha is named among the kings supporting the house, sharing only the king’s name.
ezra-7:7:7.why: Links the king’s name across passages.

ezra-7:7:8.summary: Arthasastha’s decree to Esdras authorized this journey of priests, Levites and others to Jerusalem.
ezra-7:7:8.why: Gives the decree behind the journey.

ezra-7:7:9.summary: The gatekeepers’ organization provides background for the gatekeepers among the returnees (shown text truncated).

ezra-7:9:0.summary: Esdras “came up from Babylon” with “the hand of the Lord his God” upon him, the same journey and refrain.
ezra-7:9:0.why: Same refrain of God’s hand on the journey.

ezra-7:9:1.summary: Nehemiah too credits success to “the good hand of God,” the same phrase as 7:9.
ezra-7:9:1.why: Parallel use of the good-hand refrain.

ezra-7:9:2.summary: “The hand of God, which was good upon me” closely echoes “the hand of his God was good upon him.”
ezra-7:9:2.why: Parallel use of the good-hand refrain.

ezra-7:10:0.summary: People “will seek law” from the priest’s mouth, matching Esdras the priest who set his heart to seek and teach the law.
ezra-7:10:0.why: Shows the priest’s role as teacher of law.

ezra-7:10:1.summary: Paul’s charge to proclaim and teach broadly parallels Esdras’s commitment to teach.

ezra-7:10:2.summary: Hearing and putting words into practice broadly matches Esdras’s resolve to seek the law and do it.

ezra-7:10:3.summary: Blessing for doing what one knows loosely echoes Esdras’s resolve to do the law.

ezra-7:10:4.summary: Delight and meditation in the Lord’s law broadly match Esdras’s devotion to the law.
ezra-7:10:4.why: Model of devotion to the law.

ezra-7:10:5.summary: The king commissions Esdras to appoint judges and make the law known, fulfilling his aim to teach.
ezra-7:10:5.why: Shows royal backing for Esdras’s teaching.

ezra-7:10:6.summary: Praise of the Lord’s blameless law relates generally to Esdras’s devotion to it.

ezra-7:10:7.summary: The Levitical priests “shall declare Thine ordinances … and Thy law unto Israel,” the priestly teaching Esdras undertook.

ezra-7:10:8.summary: David’s prayer to direct hearts toward God loosely relates to Esdras setting his heart on the law.
ezra-7:10:8.why: Theme of a heart directed to God.

ezra-7:10:9.summary: Esdras as a ready scribe in the law of Moses is the same person described as devoted to seeking the law.

ezra-7:10:10.summary: The Greek Psalm mentions God attending to “the preparation of their heart,” only loosely echoing Esdras preparing his heart.
ezra-7:10:10.why: Loose echo of a prepared heart.

ezra-7:10:11.summary: Speaking what fits sound teaching broadly parallels Esdras’s commitment to teach.

ezra-7:10:12.summary: The psalmist loves and seeks God’s commandments, broadly echoing Esdras seeking the law.
ezra-7:10:12.why: Devotional model of seeking the law.

ezra-7:10:13.summary: Samuel urges Israel to prepare their hearts toward the Lord, loosely like Esdras setting his heart.

ezra-7:10:14.summary: “I sought Thy commandments” broadly echoes Esdras seeking the law.
ezra-7:10:14.why: Devotional echo of seeking God’s law.

ezra-7:10:15.summary: Hezekiah encouraging Levites at the feast shares only general mention of Levites’ understanding.
ezra-7:10:15.why: No specific link to Esdras’s resolve.

ezra-7:10:16.summary: The Greek Psalm’s “my heart is ready” for praise does not specifically connect to Esdras’s study of the law.

ezra-7:10:17.summary: An overseer “able to teach” loosely parallels Esdras’s role as teacher.

ezra-7:10:18.summary: Jehoshaphat “directed your heart to seek the Lord,” loosely echoing Esdras setting his heart to seek.
ezra-7:10:18.why: Similar language of setting the heart.

ezra-7:10:19.summary: Levites and priests teach Judah with “a book of the Lord’s law,” the same teaching mission Esdras undertook.
ezra-7:10:19.why: Earlier precedent for teaching the law.

ezra-7:10:20.summary: Titus’s charge to speak with authority has no specific link to Esdras’s devotion to the law.

ezra-7:10:21.summary: Jesus’ pattern of doing and teaching loosely parallels Esdras’s resolve to do and teach the law.
ezra-7:10:21.why: Same order of doing then teaching.

ezra-7:10:22.summary: Rehoboam “did not direct his heart to seek the Lord,” contrasting with Esdras’s resolve.

ezra-7:10:23.summary: The command to keep and do the commandments generally echoes Esdras’s aim to do the law.

ezra-7:10:25.summary: Washing robes for the tree of life has no specific link to Esdras seeking and teaching the law.

ezra-7:10:26.summary: “Whoever does and teaches them” matches Esdras’s resolve to do the law and teach it.
ezra-7:10:26.why: Same pairing of doing and teaching.

ezra-7:10:27.summary: Making the heart pure before God loosely parallels Esdras preparing his heart.

ezra-7:10:28.summary: Simon “sought out the law” and removed the lawless, loosely like Esdras seeking the law.
ezra-7:10:28.why: Later leader devoted to the law.

ezra-7:10:29.summary: Sirach on the scribe’s wisdom relates generally to Esdras the scribe’s study.

ezra-7:10:30.summary: One who gives his soul to considering the law of the Most High closely portrays Esdras’s devotion to the law.

ezra-7:11:0.summary: Scribes in “Moses’ chair” loosely connect to Esdras as scribe of the Mosaic commandments.
ezra-7:11:0.why: Later scribal authority in Moses’ law.

ezra-7:11:1.summary: Esdras described as a ready scribe in the law of Moses is the same priest and scribe named in the decree.

ezra-7:11:2.summary: Jesus disputing with scribes about tradition shares only the word scribe with Esdras’s title (shown text truncated).

ezra-7:11:3.summary: “An account of the letter” introduces another Persian document, a formal parallel only.

ezra-7:11:4.summary: A letter to Arthasastha is introduced similarly, sharing the king and document formula.

ezra-7:11:5.summary: Jesus’ woe on scribes shares only the word scribe with Esdras’s title.

ezra-7:12:2.summary: Another Persian royal letter opens with a greeting formula, a formal parallel to Arthasastha’s letter.

ezra-7:12:3.summary: The Assyrian boast of being ruler has no specific link to Arthasastha’s title in the Saints text.

ezra-7:12:4.summary: Ben-Hadad with thirty-two kings shares only the idea of an overlord of kings.

ezra-7:12:5.summary: God as “King of those who reign” contrasts with the earthly “king of kings” title.
ezra-7:12:5.why: Places the royal title under God.

ezra-7:12:6.summary: Solomon ruling beyond the River shares only a geographic phrase with Arthasastha’s letter.

ezra-7:12:7.summary: Christ bears the name “King of kings,” the same title the Persian king claims.

ezra-7:12:8.summary: A letter to Arthasastha uses the same king and letter formula, a formal parallel only.

ezra-7:12:9.summary: The Lamb as “King of kings” shares the title used by Arthasastha.

ezra-7:12:10.summary: A pagan king calls Israel’s God “Lord of kings,” loosely like Arthasastha honoring the God of heaven.

ezra-7:13:0.summary: Darius “issued a decision” using the same royal formula, a parallel Persian decree favoring the Jews.

ezra-7:13:1.summary: Hezekiah’s decree inviting Israel to Jerusalem loosely parallels the decree allowing Israel to go to Jerusalem.
ezra-7:13:1.why: Royal invitation to come to Jerusalem.

ezra-7:13:2.summary: God setting an unpassing command for creation has no specific link to the king’s decree.

ezra-7:13:3.summary: God working in people to will loosely relates to those who “freely” wish to go.

ezra-7:13:4.summary: The Greek Psalm 109:3 lacks the “willing people” wording, so the assumed link does not carry.
ezra-7:13:4.why: Septuagint wording removes the intended link.
ezra-7:13:4.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

ezra-7:13:6.summary: Cyrus “issued a decision” for the house to be built, a parallel Persian decree for the return.
ezra-7:13:6.why: Earlier royal decree in the same series.

ezra-7:13:7.summary: The king’s order to hang Haman’s sons shares only the idea of a royal order.

ezra-7:13:8.summary: “The one who wisheth” may come “freely” loosely echoes those who freely wish to go.

ezra-7:13:9.summary: Haman’s decree hurried in Susa has no specific link to Arthasastha’s decree of return.

ezra-7:14:0.summary: The rulers of Persia and Media nearest the king reflect the same institution as the king’s “seven advisers.”

ezra-7:14:1.summary: Darius decreeing honor for Daniel’s God loosely parallels a Persian king authorizing God’s law.

ezra-7:14:2.summary: The next verse mentions the same king and advisers offering silver and gold, continuing the decree.

ezra-7:14:3.summary: Cyrus’s decree concerning Jerusalem in Judea loosely parallels this commission for Judea and Jerusalem.

ezra-7:14:4.summary: The king calling to Daniel at the lions’ den shares no specific element with Esdras’s commission.

ezra-7:14:5.summary: A ruler keeping a copy of the law loosely relates to the law of God being in Esdras’s hand.
ezra-7:14:5.why: Ruling according to the written law.

ezra-7:14:7.summary: A pagan king honoring Israel’s God broadly matches Persian recognition of God’s law.

ezra-7:14:8.summary: The offering of “the king, his advisers” for the house shows the same king and advisers acting.

ezra-7:14:9.summary: The Greek Isaiah 8:20 on law given for help does not specifically connect to Esdras’s commission.
ezra-7:14:9.why: Septuagint wording carries no clear link.

ezra-7:14:10.summary: Esdras is told to judge by “the wisdom of God in your hand” and enforce the law, continuing the same commission.

ezra-7:14:11.summary: Darius’s decree protecting the house is another Persian decree, only loosely related to Esdras’s inspection.

ezra-7:14:12.summary: Officials reporting on Judea’s temple work loosely parallels sending Esdras to inspect Judea.

ezra-7:15:0.summary: Solomon built a house for God’s dwelling, broadly underlying the God who dwells in Jerusalem.
ezra-7:15:0.why: Background of the temple as God’s dwelling.

ezra-7:15:1.summary: “He who dwells in Jerusalem” matches the decree’s description of God who dwells in Jerusalem.

ezra-7:15:2.summary: Darius’s “God whose name dwells there” parallels Arthasastha’s God “who dwells in Jerusalem.”

ezra-7:15:3.summary: Nations bring “silver and gold” to glorify God’s house, matching royal silver and gold for the Lord’s house.
ezra-7:15:3.why: Prophecy of foreign wealth for the temple.

ezra-7:15:4.summary: “Kings will bring Thee gifts” to the sanctuary over Jerusalem matches a king offering silver and gold.

ezra-7:15:5.summary: God’s dwelling in Zion broadly echoes God “who dwells in Jerusalem.”
ezra-7:15:5.why: Theme of God’s dwelling in Zion.

ezra-7:15:6.summary: God chose Jerusalem for His name, broadly relating to God dwelling in Jerusalem.
ezra-7:15:6.why: Background on Jerusalem as chosen place.

ezra-7:15:7.summary: The Lord “who dwells in Zion” loosely echoes God dwelling in Jerusalem.

ezra-7:15:8.summary: Those around God bring gifts, broadly matching the freely offered silver and gold.
ezra-7:15:8.why: Theme of gifts brought to God.

ezra-7:15:9.summary: Foreign kings offering gifts closely fits a Persian king offering silver and gold to Israel’s God.

ezra-7:15:10.summary: Love for God’s house and dwelling loosely relates to gifts for the Lord’s house.

ezra-7:15:11.summary: Solomon’s humility about building God a house only broadly relates to gifts for the Lord’s house.

ezra-7:15:12.summary: Darius likewise ordered royal funds for the house and offerings, a direct precedent for Arthasastha’s gift.

ezra-7:15:13.summary: Rulers and the king’s stewards “offered eagerly” for the temple, paralleling free royal offerings for the house.
ezra-7:15:13.why: Parallel freewill giving for the temple.

ezra-7:15:14.summary: Cyrus’s order that expense be paid “from the king’s house” parallels royal silver and gold for the house.

ezra-7:15:15.summary: Kings bringing their glory into the city broadly echoes kings giving to God’s house.

ezra-7:16:0.summary: Leaders “offered eagerly” for the temple, paralleling the voluntary offering of people and priests.
ezra-7:16:0.why: Parallel freewill giving for the temple.

ezra-7:16:1.summary: Silver, gold and “the freewill offering for the house of God in Jerusalem” closely matches this verse.
ezra-7:16:1.why: Same pattern of gifts from exile.

ezra-7:16:2.summary: The people “offered eagerly to the Lord with a full heart,” paralleling voluntary offerings for the house.

ezra-7:16:3.summary: Neighbors gave silver, gold and “freewill offerings,” the same pattern of support from exile.
ezra-7:16:3.why: Same pattern of gifts from exile.

ezra-7:16:4.summary: David and the people “offer eagerly” for the temple, matching freely offered gifts for God’s house.

ezra-7:16:5.summary: Giving acceptable by readiness broadly relates to voluntary offerings.
ezra-7:16:5.why: New Testament principle of willing giving.

ezra-7:16:7.summary: Giving without compulsion as a cheerful giver broadly parallels voluntary offerings.
ezra-7:16:7.why: New Testament principle of willing giving.

ezra-7:17:0.summary: Offerings brought to the place God chose for His name (shown text truncated) underlie offering sacrifices at the Jerusalem altar.
ezra-7:17:0.why: Mosaic basis for the central altar.

ezra-7:17:1.summary: Darius’s provision of cattle, rams, lambs and wine for offerings parallels Arthasastha’s provision of bulls, rams and lambs.

ezra-7:17:3.summary: Silver carried to the chosen place is spent on cattle, sheep and wine, as Esdras buys animals and drink offerings.
ezra-7:17:3.why: Law on converting silver to offerings.

ezra-7:17:4.summary: Temple traders selling oxen and sheep share only the animals; no real connection to the decree.

ezra-7:17:5.summary: Jesus cleansing the temple has no specific link to purchasing sacrifices under the decree.

ezra-7:18:0.summary: The decree’s enforcement clause is in the same letter but adds little to the freedom over remaining silver.

ezra-7:18:1.summary: Understanding the Lord’s will loosely echoes doing “as is pleasing to your God.”

ezra-7:18:2.summary: Temple silver was entrusted without accounting “in their trustworthiness,” paralleling the discretion given Esdras.
ezra-7:18:2.why: Precedent of trusted handling of temple funds.

ezra-7:18:3.summary: No account was demanded for the silver because they acted faithfully, paralleling trust in Esdras’s use of funds.
ezra-7:18:3.why: Precedent of trusted handling of temple funds.

ezra-7:19:0.summary: Speaking against “the God of Jerusalem” shares only that phrase; the context of blasphemy is unrelated.

ezra-7:19:2.summary: Jerusalem as the Lord’s throne has no specific connection to delivering the temple vessels.

ezra-7:20:0.summary: Cyrus’s order that expense be paid “from the king’s house” parallels provision from the king’s treasury houses.

ezra-7:21:0.summary: “The king granted him his requests” describes the same royal provision for Esdras.

ezra-7:21:1.summary: Opponents warned the king against Jerusalem’s rebuilding, contrasting with Arthasastha’s generous decree.

ezra-7:21:2.summary: Darius’s orders to officials “beyond the river” parallel Arthasastha’s decree to treasuries beyond the river.
ezra-7:21:2.why: Parallel royal orders to regional officials.

ezra-7:21:3.summary: The same decree of Arthasastha to Esdras, “scribe of the law of the God of heaven,” provides context.

ezra-7:21:4.summary: Taxes from the region west of the river relate loosely to the treasuries beyond the river.

ezra-7:22:0.summary: Both name “a hundred kors of wheat” and a hundred measures of oil, but the parable's debts have no connection to Artaxerxes' grant.
ezra-7:22:0.why: Shows the same standard commodity measures in use.

ezra-7:22:1.summary: The king's unlimited salt would supply sacrifices that the law requires to be “seasoned with salt”.
ezra-7:22:1.why: Explains why salt is included in the temple grant.

ezra-7:22:2.summary: Ezekiel sets measures of oil for offerings, while Ezra gives a royal allowance of oil; the only link is temple supplies.
ezra-7:22:2.why: Background on oil measures for worship.

ezra-7:23:0.summary: Both stress diligent obedience to God's command, but the psalm is a general statement about keeping commandments.
ezra-7:23:0.why: Echoes the call to carry out God's decree carefully.

ezra-7:23:1.summary: Zechariah speaks of nations gathering against Jerusalem; it shares nothing specific with the king's concern to avoid wrath.

ezra-7:23:2.summary: Same royal letter of Artaxerxes: the king's “decision” permits the return, matching the decree about the house of God.
ezra-7:23:2.why: Places the verse within the same decree.

ezra-7:23:4.summary: Same letter: Esdras may use the remaining silver and gold as pleases his God, alongside the order to do God's decision.
ezra-7:23:4.why: Context from the same royal decree.

ezra-7:24:0.summary: Same list of temple personnel: priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and Nathinim who went up with Esdras.
ezra-7:24:0.why: Identifies who receives the tax exemption.

ezra-7:24:1.summary: Earlier the enemies warned there would be “no taxes” for the king; now the king himself forbids taxing temple ministers.
ezra-7:24:1.why: Shows the reversal of royal policy on taxes.

ezra-7:24:2.summary: Both concern taxes and tribute in the region, but Ezra 4:20 recalls past kings collecting revenue, not exemption.
ezra-7:24:2.why: Background on taxation beyond the river.

ezra-7:24:3.summary: The shown list enumerates priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers, the same classes exempted from tax.
ezra-7:24:3.why: Lists the groups named in the exemption.

ezra-7:25:0.summary: Esdras resolved to seek the law and to teach ordinances in Israel, matching his commission to teach those who do not know.
ezra-7:25:0.why: Shows Esdras was prepared for this task.

ezra-7:25:2.summary: Esdras acts by the “wisdom of God”, and James says God gives wisdom to those who ask; a general theme only.
ezra-7:25:2.why: Wisdom for leadership comes from God.

ezra-7:25:3.summary: A priest's lips guard knowledge and people seek law from him, matching the priest Esdras teaching the law.
ezra-7:25:3.why: Defines the teaching role Esdras fulfills.

ezra-7:25:4.summary: The Lord's law makes infants wise, loosely echoing making the law known to those who do not know it.
ezra-7:25:4.why: Value of the law for the unlearned.

ezra-7:25:5.summary: Describes wisdom from above as impartial and peaceable, a general fit for judges but with no specific link.
ezra-7:25:5.why: Qualities of godly wisdom in judgment.

ezra-7:25:6.summary: The people read the book of the law of the Lord, a later outcome of teaching the law, but no specific link.
ezra-7:25:6.why: Shows the law being read publicly.

ezra-7:25:7.summary: David appointed “scribes and judges”, the same pair of offices Esdras is told to appoint.
ezra-7:25:7.why: Precedent for appointing scribes and judges.

ezra-7:25:8.summary: Jehoshaphat sent leaders, Levites and priests with the book of the Lord's law to teach the people in Judah's cities.
ezra-7:25:8.why: Earlier royal program of teaching the law.

ezra-7:25:9.summary: Esdras and the Levites read God's law and explained it so the people understood, carrying out making it known.
ezra-7:25:9.why: Shows Esdras fulfilling his teaching commission.

ezra-7:25:10.summary: Esdras brings and reads the law of Moses to all who could understand, fulfilling the charge to teach the law.
ezra-7:25:10.why: Narrates Esdras teaching the law publicly.

ezra-7:25:11.summary: Both are royal orders addressed to officials “beyond the river”, but Darius's command concerns noninterference with the temple.

ezra-7:25:12.summary: Scribes sitting in Moses' chair teach the law, loosely related to Esdras appointing scribes who know the law.

ezra-7:25:13.summary: The Lord gives wisdom, matching the “wisdom of God” in Esdras' hand only at a general level.
ezra-7:25:13.why: Source of the wisdom Esdras uses.

ezra-7:25:14.summary: God's discernment in Solomon enabled justice, loosely parallel to judging by God's wisdom.

ezra-7:25:15.summary: Jehoshaphat appointed priests and Levites to judge and instruct people in ordinances and judgments, closely matching Esdras' charge.
ezra-7:25:15.why: Earlier model of appointing judges by the law.

ezra-7:25:16.summary: The law is a lamp and light, a general statement about the law's value without a specific link.

ezra-7:25:17.summary: Jesus teaches the crowd out of compassion, loosely paralleling teaching those who do not know.

ezra-7:25:18.summary: Same letter: the law of God “in your hand”, matching the wisdom of God in Esdras' hand.

ezra-7:25:19.summary: David prays the Lord will give Solomon wisdom to keep the law, a general parallel to wisdom and law.
ezra-7:25:19.why: Wisdom given for keeping God's law.

ezra-7:25:20.summary: Paul asks how people can hear without someone proclaiming, loosely echoing making the law known to the ignorant.
ezra-7:25:20.why: Need for teachers to be sent.

ezra-7:25:21.summary: The law of Moses is read to the people, an outcome of the teaching program, but unrelated in specifics.
ezra-7:25:21.why: Shows the law being read and applied.

ezra-7:25:22.summary: Moses appoints able men as rulers who “judge the people”, the founding pattern for appointing judges.

ezra-7:25:23.summary: A scribe trained for the kingdom brings out treasure, related only through the scribal role.

ezra-7:25:24.summary: God's commandments make one wiser than teachers, loosely linked to wisdom and the law.

ezra-7:26:0.summary: Another Persian decree threatens punishment, with house confiscated and impalement, for anyone who disobeys the king's word.

ezra-7:26:1.summary: Shown text gives laws against false prophets; it shares only the idea of punishment for breaking God's law.

ezra-7:26:2.summary: Shown text sets death penalties in the law; the link to Artaxerxes' penalties is only general.
ezra-7:26:2.why: Death penalty in the law of God.

ezra-7:26:3.summary: Shown text begins with slave laws, sharing nothing specific with the decree's penalties; judged on truncated text.

ezra-7:26:4.summary: A pagan king decrees reverence for the God of Israel, similar to Artaxerxes enforcing God's law, but different specifics.

ezra-7:26:5.summary: Judah carries out the king's ordinance according to the Lord's word, a loose pairing of royal and divine law.

ezra-7:26:6.summary: Nebuchadnezzar decrees dismemberment and confiscation of house for blaspheming God, a parallel royal penalty decree.
ezra-7:26:6.why: Another king enforcing honor of God.

ezra-7:26:7.summary: The psalm calls for God to uproot a wicked man; it has no specific link to the decree's penalties.

ezra-7:27:0.summary: God “put it into their hearts” to do His purpose, a verbal echo of God putting it in the king's heart.

ezra-7:27:1.summary: The Lord turned the heart of the king toward them to strengthen work on God's house, closely matching this blessing.
ezra-7:27:1.why: Earlier instance of God moving a king's heart.

ezra-7:27:2.summary: Lebanon's glory comes “to glorify My holy place”, echoing the king's purpose to glorify the Lord's house.
ezra-7:27:2.why: Prophetic hope of glorifying the temple.

ezra-7:27:3.summary: Nehemiah speaks of what God was putting into his heart, echoing God putting it in the king's heart.
ezra-7:27:3.why: God prompting hearts for Jerusalem's restoration.

ezra-7:27:4.summary: Thanks be to God “who put” diligence in Titus' heart, a close parallel to blessing God who put it in the king's heart.

ezra-7:27:5.summary: The king grants Nehemiah's request by the good hand of God, another Persian king moved to support Jerusalem.
ezra-7:27:5.why: Parallel royal favor credited to God.

ezra-7:27:6.summary: God puts His laws upon hearts, sharing only the image of God putting something in the heart.

ezra-7:27:7.summary: Every good gift is from above, a general basis for thanking God for the king's favor.

ezra-7:27:8.summary: God inscribes His laws upon hearts, a loose verbal echo of God placing intent in a heart.

ezra-7:27:9.summary: Paul rejoices in the Philippians' renewed concern; there is no specific link to God moving the king.

ezra-7:27:10.summary: David blesses the Lord, God of Israel, for provision toward the house, a parallel blessing formula over temple giving.
ezra-7:27:10.why: Model of blessing God for temple provision.

ezra-7:27:12.summary: “God put it into my heart”, Nehemiah says, closely echoing God putting it in the king's heart.

ezra-7:28:0.summary: “The Lord… strengthened me”, Paul says, echoing Esdras being strengthened, but the setting differs entirely.

ezra-7:28:1.summary: God's eyes were upon the captives during the Persian inquiry, a general theme of divine favor under Persian rule.

ezra-7:28:2.summary: Jacob's renaming shares only the idea of being strong; no real connection to Esdras' favor with the king.

ezra-7:28:3.summary: Same narrator uses “the hand of our God was good upon us” for the Levites who joined him.

ezra-7:28:4.summary: God “inclined mercy toward us” before the Persian kings, the same phrase Esdras uses here.
ezra-7:28:4.why: Same expression of royal favor from God.

ezra-7:28:5.summary: Nehemiah's request was granted “according to the good hand of God”, the same formula Esdras uses.
ezra-7:28:5.why: Parallel favor from a Persian king.

ezra-7:28:6.summary: The journey succeeded “because the hand of his God was good upon him”, the same formula about Esdras.

ezra-7:28:7.summary: Jacob prays God will give grace before the ruler, loosely similar to mercy in the king's eyes.

ezra-7:28:8.summary: The king granted Esdras' requests because the hand of the Lord his God was upon him, the same event and formula.

ezra-7:28:9.summary: A proclamation from Nineveh's king and nobles shares only the pairing of king and officials.

ezra-7:28:10.summary: Nehemiah prays for compassion before the king he serves, paralleling Esdras receiving mercy before the king.

ezra-7:28:11.summary: Names the king and his “seven advisers”, the same counselors before whom Esdras found mercy.

ezra-8:1:0.summary: Reports the same group going up with Esdras in the reign of Arthasastha.

ezra-8:1:1.summary: Some returnees could not find their family record; related only through genealogical listing.

ezra-8:1:2.summary: The king's decree allowing Israelites to go with Esdras authorizes this group going up.

ezra-8:1:3.summary: “The leaders of the families” arose to go up in the first return, parallel to the leaders who came with Esdras.
ezra-8:1:3.why: Earlier return led by family heads.

ezra-8:1:4.summary: Israel was recorded by enrollment, including the deportees to Babylon; related to genealogical listing only.

ezra-8:1:5.summary: Ancestral rulers of priests and Levites are listed, related only by the idea of family heads.

ezra-8:1:6.summary: Simeon's settlements and enrollment have no specific link to Esdras' list of leaders.

ezra-8:1:7.summary: A count of Uzziah's ancestral rulers for war shares only the phrase ancestral rulers.

ezra-8:1:8.summary: Heads of families give to the treasury in Nehemiah's day; related only through family leaders of the return.

ezra-8:1:9.summary: Levitical ancestral rulers living in Jerusalem; only a general genealogy-leadership link.

ezra-8:1:10.summary: David's ancestral rulers over the Transjordan tribes share only the phrase about family heads.

ezra-8:2:0.summary: Chattous, son of Samaia of David's line, matches “Atous” from the sons of David.

ezra-8:2:1.summary: Shown genealogy names Phinees and Ithamar as Aaron's line, the priestly houses of Gersom and Daniel.

ezra-8:2:2.summary: David's son Daniel shares only a name with the priest Daniel of Ithamar's line.
ezra-8:2:2.why: Different person with the same name.

ezra-8:3:1.summary: The sons of Phoros appear in the earlier return list, the same family as here.
ezra-8:3:1.why: Earlier members of the same clan.

ezra-8:3:2.summary: Phoros appears among the people's rulers sealing the covenant, the same family.
