ezra-9:1:23.summary: The Ammonite and Moabite are not to enter the assembly, the law behind including them here.

ezra-9:1:24.summary: Names the Amorite, Hittite, Perizzite, Canaanite and Jebusite, overlapping with this list.

ezra-9:1:25.summary: Do not be unequally yoked; come out from their midst and be separated, the same call to separation.

ezra-9:1:26.summary: Solomon took Moabite, Ammonite, Hittite and Amorite wives, the same nations and the same failing.

ezra-9:1:27.summary: Those “separating himself from the uncleanness of the nations of the land”, the separation now neglected.

ezra-9:1:28.summary: Opponents of the wall, including Ammanites, share only an ethnic name.

ezra-9:2:0.summary: Jews married Ammanite and Moabite wives and their children lost their language, a parallel case.

ezra-9:2:1.summary: Sechenias confesses settling foreign wives from the peoples of the land, the same sin.

ezra-9:2:2.summary: Lists priests and Levites who had settled foreign wives, naming those involved in this offense.

ezra-9:2:3.summary: Forbids taking their daughters for your sons, lest they lead them to other gods, the very law broken here.

ezra-9:2:5.summary: Israel is “a holy people” chosen above all nations, the basis of the “holy seed”.

ezra-9:2:6.summary: Israel is “a holy people” chosen out of the nations, underlying the term holy seed.

ezra-9:2:7.summary: Judah profaned the Lord's holy things and devoted himself to foreign gods, addressing the same sin.
ezra-9:2:7.why: Prophetic rebuke of the same sin.

ezra-9:2:8.summary: Israel as a holy nation, a general basis for holy seed.

ezra-9:2:9.summary: God seeks offspring and faithfulness to one's wife, a general link to marriage and seed.

ezra-9:2:10.summary: Paul says children of mixed marriages are holy, contrasting with the holy seed being led astray.

ezra-9:2:11.summary: “You shall be holy people to Me”, a general holiness theme.

ezra-9:2:12.summary: The mixed population was separated, and the priest Eliasib drew close to Tobia, a parallel problem among leaders.

ezra-9:2:13.summary: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers, a general parallel to forbidden marriages.

ezra-9:2:14.summary: Sons of God took wives from the daughters of men, a loose parallel of illicit marriages.

ezra-9:2:15.summary: A high priest's son was son-in-law of Sanaballat, showing leaders foremost in mixed marriage.

ezra-9:2:16.summary: Nehemiah rebukes Sabbath profanation, a different offense.

ezra-9:2:17.summary: The shown Greek-based text has a remnant as plunder like a terebinth, without the “holy seed” wording the label assumes.
ezra-9:2:17.why: Link not present in this wording.

ezra-9:3:0.summary: “When I heard these words, I sat down” and mourned, closely parallel to Esdras' grief on hearing.

ezra-9:3:1.summary: Joshua tore his clothes before the Lord over Israel's sin, a parallel mourning act.

ezra-9:3:2.summary: Shame and baldness on every head, general mourning imagery.

ezra-9:3:3.summary: The king did not tear his garments on hearing God's words, contrasting with Esdras' response.

ezra-9:3:4.summary: A troubled spirit and heart, a general distress theme.

ezra-9:3:5.summary: Ezekiel sat seven days among the exiles, loosely echoing sitting in stunned silence.

ezra-9:3:6.summary: Job's friends tore their robes and sat silent, closely parallel to tearing garments and sitting quietly.

ezra-9:3:7.summary: Every head and beard shaved in mourning, a general parallel to tearing hair and beard.

ezra-9:3:8.summary: Daniel trembles and is astonished for an hour, loosely echoing Esdras shaking with agitation.

ezra-9:3:9.summary: Praise of God's fearsome works shares nothing specific with Esdras' grief.

ezra-9:3:10.summary: Baldness on every head in Moab's mourning, general mourning imagery.

ezra-9:3:11.summary: Daniel was undone by a vision, a loose parallel to being overwhelmed.

ezra-9:3:12.summary: Job tore his garments and cut his hair, the same two mourning acts.

ezra-9:3:13.summary: Prohibits shaving the head and beard in mourning, background to hair rites.

ezra-9:3:14.summary: Shave and shear hair in grief, general mourning imagery.

ezra-9:3:15.summary: Shear your head and lament over a rejected generation, a mourning gesture over sin.

ezra-9:3:16.summary: Over the same sin of intermarriage, Nehemiah pulled out others' hair, whereas Esdras plucked his own.
ezra-9:3:16.why: Contrasting responses to the same sin.

ezra-9:3:17.summary: “When King Hezekiah heard, he tore his garments”, closely parallel to Esdras' response.

ezra-9:4:0.summary: The proposal to make a covenant and put away the wives continues the same crisis over the covenant-breaking.

ezra-9:4:1.summary: God looks to one who trembles at His words; the Greek-based source says “pursued the word”, so the echo is only loose.

ezra-9:4:2.summary: Prescribes the evening lamb, background to the evening sacrifice.

ezra-9:4:3.summary: Weeping because the law is not kept, a general grief over disobedience.

ezra-9:4:4.summary: Those who grieve over lawlessness are marked, loosely like those gathering over the covenant-breaking.

ezra-9:4:5.summary: Josiah humbled himself and tore his garments on hearing God's words, a general parallel.

ezra-9:4:6.summary: The ninth hour of prayer at the temple, related to the time of the evening sacrifice.

ezra-9:4:7.summary: “At the hour of the evening sacrifice” Daniel prays, the same time marker as here.

ezra-9:5:0.summary: Solomon “spread his hands toward heaven” in prayer, matching Esdras stretching out his hands toward the Lord God.
ezra-9:5:0.why: Shows the outstretched-hands gesture of public penitential prayer.

ezra-9:5:1.summary: Solomon envisions supplicants “spreading his hands toward this house” in affliction, the very posture Esdras takes in his distress.
ezra-9:5:1.why: Esdras's prayer fits Solomon's template for prayer toward the temple.

ezra-9:5:3.summary: Moses will “spread out my hands to the Lord”; shared prayer gesture only, in an unrelated plague context.

ezra-9:5:4.summary: Moses “spread out his hands to the Lord”; same gesture of prayer but no confession or repentance context.
ezra-9:5:4.why: Another example of the prayer gesture.

ezra-9:5:5.summary: Paul's “I bend my knees before the Father” closely echoes Esdras's “I bend upon my knees” before God.
ezra-9:5:5.why: Same kneeling posture of earnest intercession.

ezra-9:5:6.summary: Solomon “fell on his knees” and “spread out his hands toward heaven” before the assembly, the same double posture as Esdras.
ezra-9:5:6.why: Close parallel of kneeling, outstretched public prayer.

ezra-9:5:7.summary: Call to “bow down and fall before Him” and weep; general posture of humility in worship.
ezra-9:5:7.why: Loose parallel of bodily humility before God.

ezra-9:5:8.summary: “The lifting of my hands as an evening sacrifice” matches Esdras praying with outstretched hands at the evening sacrifice.
ezra-9:5:8.why: Links prayer with hands to the evening sacrifice hour.

ezra-9:5:9.summary: “I spread out my hands unto Thee” echoes Esdras stretching out his hands toward the Lord in need.

ezra-9:5:10.summary: Jesus “knelt down, and prayed”; kneeling in prayer is the only shared element.

ezra-9:5:11.summary: God refuses those who “stretch your hands toward Me” with bloody hands, contrasting Esdras's penitent outstretched hands.
ezra-9:5:11.why: Shows the gesture is empty without repentance.

ezra-9:5:12.summary: Disciples “knelt on the beach and prayed”; only the kneeling posture is shared.

ezra-9:6:0.summary: Babylon's “sins have piled up as far as heaven” echoes Esdras's “offenses have grown to heaven.”
ezra-9:6:0.why: Same image of sins heaped up to heaven.

ezra-9:6:1.summary: “My lawless deeds rose above my head” closely matches “our lawless deeds have multiplied above our heads.”
ezra-9:6:1.why: Near-identical image of guilt overwhelming the penitent.

ezra-9:6:2.summary: Oded says the killing in anger “has reached the heavens”; similar image but of Israel's wrath, not confessed guilt.
ezra-9:6:2.why: Parallel hyperbole of wrongdoing reaching heaven.

ezra-9:6:3.summary: The prodigal confesses sin “against heaven” and unworthiness; general theme of shamed confession.

ezra-9:6:4.summary: Job “despised myself” as earth and ashes; general self-abasement, not communal guilt.

ezra-9:6:5.summary: Conclusion of the same prayer of Esdras: “Here we are before Thee in our offenses.”
ezra-9:6:5.why: Frames the prayer's opening and closing confession.

ezra-9:6:6.summary: “We lay down in our shame…we sinned…we and our fathers…until this day” parallels Esdras's shame and generational guilt.

ezra-9:6:9.summary: Job feels he is nothing and covers his mouth; humility but no shame for sins.
ezra-9:6:9.why: Loose parallel of speechlessness before God.

ezra-9:6:10.summary: Israel will “remember and be ashamed” of what it has done; shared shame over sin.
ezra-9:6:10.why: Shame as the fitting response to forgiven sin.

ezra-9:6:11.summary: Ephraim repents and groans over “days of shame”; general repentant shame.

ezra-9:6:12.summary: “Our lawlessness is great before Thee…our lawless deeds are within us” parallels Esdras's communal confession of multiplied lawless deeds.

ezra-9:6:13.summary: People who were “not at all ashamed” contrast with Esdras who is “ashamed and abashed.”

ezra-9:6:14.summary: Notes Sodom's wickedness before God; no shared wording or confession beyond generic sin.

ezra-9:6:15.summary: Later line of the same prayer acknowledging “our evil deeds and our great offense.”

ezra-9:6:16.summary: Israel was “shameless toward everyone,” contrasting Esdras's shame.

ezra-9:6:17.summary: Promise to whiten scarlet sins; general sin-and-forgiveness theme only.

ezra-9:6:18.summary: Paul speaks of things “of which you are now ashamed”; general shame over past sin.

ezra-9:7:0.summary: Hezekiah confesses “our fathers departed and did what was evil”; generational guilt, though punishment not shown.
ezra-9:7:0.why: Parallel acknowledgment of the fathers' sin.

ezra-9:7:1.summary: Daniel's “shame of face…as on this day” to “our kings, rulers, and fathers” closely parallels Esdras's confession.

ezra-9:7:2.summary: Song of Moses on Jacob forsaking God (truncated); general background to Israel's long apostasy.

ezra-9:7:3.summary: Jesus says hearers “fill up the measure of your fathers”; generational guilt theme only.

ezra-9:7:4.summary: “We sinned with our fathers; we acted lawlessly” matches Esdras's confession of guilt from the days of the fathers.
ezra-9:7:4.why: Same solidarity with the fathers' sin.

ezra-9:7:5.summary: Samaria deported to the Assyrians “because the Israelites sinned”; an example of captivity for sin.
ezra-9:7:5.why: Historical instance of exile for sin.

ezra-9:7:6.summary: “Our fathers sinned…we bore their lawless acts” matches Esdras's generational confession of lawless deeds.
ezra-9:7:6.why: Same theme of bearing the fathers' sins.

ezra-9:7:7.summary: Moses foresees Israel turning to foreign gods (truncated); general prediction of apostasy.

ezra-9:7:8.summary: Covenant curses for disobedience (truncated; shown text has defeat before enemies); general background.
ezra-9:7:8.why: Covenant basis for the judgments named.

ezra-9:7:9.summary: Daniel confesses calamities “came upon us, because we sinned,” paralleling Esdras's captivity-for-sin confession.

ezra-9:7:10.summary: Hardship of “our kings, rulers, priests…fathers…until this day” parallels Esdras's kings and fathers in offense until this day.

ezra-9:7:11.summary: Samaria deported because they “did not listen”; general instance of exile for sin.

ezra-9:7:12.summary: Jerusalem and Judah's kings made a desolation and hissing; general judgment theme.

ezra-9:7:13.summary: Land became a desolation because of wickedness, “as on this day,” echoing Esdras's “as on this day.”
ezra-9:7:13.why: Same formula tying present ruin to sin.

ezra-9:7:14.summary: Moses warns that turning to other gods means perishing; general covenant warning.

ezra-9:7:15.summary: Sons “risen in your fathers' place” to add to God's anger; generational sin theme.
ezra-9:7:15.why: Loose parallel of continuing the fathers' sin.

ezra-9:7:16.summary: Moses warns Israel will be scattered among the nations for lawlessness; general background.

ezra-9:7:17.summary: “We are slaves today” under “kings…because of our sins” parallels being handed to kings of the nations.

ezra-9:7:18.summary: Fathers who departed were delivered “to devastation, as you see,” paralleling Esdras's handing over “as on this day.”
ezra-9:7:18.why: Same reasoning from the fathers' fate.

ezra-9:7:19.summary: The Lord's hand will be against “you and your king”; general warning only.

ezra-9:7:20.summary: “Do not become like your fathers” who did not listen; generational sin theme.
ezra-9:7:20.why: Shared postexilic reflection on the fathers.

ezra-9:7:22.summary: “Thou gavest them into the hand of the peoples of the land” parallels being “handed over into the hand of the kings of the nations.”
ezra-9:7:22.why: Close wording in a parallel confession.

ezra-9:7:23.summary: Stephen accuses hearers of resisting “as your fathers did”; generational guilt theme.

ezra-9:7:24.summary: God warns He will remove Israel from the land if they turn away; general background (truncated).

ezra-9:7:25.summary: Judah given to Chaldean raiders because of Manasseh's sins; an instance of being handed to foreign kings.

ezra-9:7:26.summary: Nations ask why the land was struck (truncated); general covenant judgment.

ezra-9:7:27.summary: Covenant curses for disobedience (truncated); general background to captivity and shame.

ezra-9:8:0.summary: “Give light to my eyes” matches Esdras's “to enlighten our eyes” as God's gift of renewed life.

ezra-9:8:1.summary: Paul's “remnant according to an election of grace” parallels survivors left by God's leniency.
ezra-9:8:1.why: Theological development of the remnant idea.

ezra-9:8:2.summary: God will “restore us” and we will “live”; general revival theme.

ezra-9:8:3.summary: “In wrath Thou wilt remember mercy”; general theme of mercy amid judgment.

ezra-9:8:4.summary: God gives “life to the brokenhearted”; general revival theme.
ezra-9:8:4.why: Loose parallel of God reviving the lowly.

ezra-9:8:5.summary: Dry bones of Israel revived and placed on their land; broad theme of national revival.

ezra-9:8:6.summary: “Thou wilt…give us life”; general plea for revival.

ezra-9:8:7.summary: The peg image of the Hebrew is absent; Saints has a ruler in “a trustworthy place,” unrelated to Esdras's “support.”
ezra-9:8:7.why: Link depends on Hebrew wording not present.

ezra-9:8:8.summary: A “pillar in the temple” has no real tie to Esdras's “support in the place of His sanctuary.”

ezra-9:8:9.summary: “Amid affliction, Thou wilt keep me alive”; general theme of preservation.
ezra-9:8:9.why: Loose parallel of revival in distress.

ezra-9:8:10.summary: “The remnant will be saved”; general remnant theme.

ezra-9:8:11.summary: “Planted nails” relates to a Hebrew peg image absent from Saints Esdras, which reads “support.”

ezra-9:8:12.summary: God rescued the soul from death to live “in light”; general rescue-and-light theme.
ezra-9:8:12.why: Loose parallel of enlightenment and life.

ezra-9:8:13.summary: Mentions “this people's remnant”; shared remnant term only.

ezra-9:8:14.summary: God in compassion “didst not make an end of them”; general mercy-in-judgment theme.

ezra-9:8:15.summary: Saints Zechariah lacks the Hebrew peg; nothing links to Esdras's “support.”

ezra-9:8:16.summary: God gives “My people's remnant” an inheritance; remnant theme only.

ezra-9:8:17.summary: A place “in My house” for outsiders; only a loose sanctuary-place link.

ezra-9:8:18.summary: “If the Lord Sabaoth had not left us seed” parallels the Lord “leaving some of us for deliverance.”
ezra-9:8:18.why: Same idea of a God-preserved remnant.

ezra-9:8:19.summary: Judah's remainder in Egypt “will not be saved”; contrasting remnant theme.
ezra-9:8:19.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

ezra-9:8:20.summary: “Few of us remain out of many”; survivor theme.
ezra-9:8:20.why: Loose parallel of a small remnant.

ezra-9:8:21.summary: “Rescued survivors are left in her”; general survivor theme.

ezra-9:8:22.summary: “Approach Him and be enlightened”; general enlightenment idiom.

ezra-9:8:23.summary: “Survivors of the sword among the nations”; general survivor theme.

ezra-9:8:24.summary: Nehemiah asks for “compassion before this man”; similar to favor before kings, not this verse's content.

ezra-9:8:25.summary: “The rescued remnant…shall again take root”; general remnant revival theme.

ezra-9:8:26.summary: Saints “my eyes have seen” lacks the Hebrew brightened-eyes idiom; no real link to “enlighten our eyes.”

ezra-9:8:27.summary: “A prayer for the remnant that remains”; remnant term only.

ezra-9:8:28.summary: Same prayer: “given us deliverance” and “we have been left as survivors” continue this verse's thought.
ezra-9:8:28.why: Develops the remnant theme within the prayer.

ezra-9:8:29.summary: Saints “His eyes looked up” does not carry the brightened-eyes idiom; no real link.

ezra-9:8:30.summary: Next verse repeats “revival” and “slavery,” explaining God's mercy through the Persian kings.

ezra-9:9:0.summary: “In our humiliation the Lord remembered us” and redeemed us; general mercy-in-lowliness theme.
ezra-9:9:0.why: Echoes God not abandoning the lowly.

ezra-9:9:1.summary: The king granted Esdras's requests because God's hand was on him, an instance of mercy before Persian kings.

ezra-9:9:2.summary: Zerubbabel's hands laid “this house's foundation” and will complete it, matching raising up the house of God.
ezra-9:9:2.why: Prophetic word on the temple's rebuilding.

ezra-9:9:3.summary: God “granted them compassions before all who had taken them captive,” matching mercy toward us before the Persian kings.

ezra-9:9:4.summary: “My house is desolate” matches restoring the temple's “desolate places.”

ezra-9:9:5.summary: God as “a wall of fire around” Jerusalem; loosely parallels God giving a fence in Judah and Jerusalem.

ezra-9:9:8.summary: “We are slaves today” under foreign kings matches “we are slaves” in Esdras.

ezra-9:9:9.summary: “I put a fence around it” shares the word fence, but for a vineyard parable.

ezra-9:9:10.summary: “You will build Jerusalem as a city”; general restoration theme.

ezra-9:9:11.summary: Cyrus king of the Persians returns the Lord's house vessels, an instance of Persian kings' favor.

ezra-9:9:12.summary: Cyrus and Darius decree “let the house be built,” exactly the Persian help to raise God's house.
ezra-9:9:12.why: Documents the royal decree behind rebuilding.

ezra-9:9:13.summary: God will “remove its fence”; contrasts with God giving a fence, shared word only.
ezra-9:9:13.why: Contrast of fence removed and restored.

ezra-9:9:14.summary: Arthasastha's decree supporting Esdras and the Lord's house, an instance of mercy before Persian kings (truncated).

ezra-9:9:15.summary: God as “a little sanctuary” in exile; loose link to God not abandoning them.

ezra-9:9:16.summary: Notes arrival in Jerusalem; only background narrative.

ezra-9:10:0.summary: “Every mouth may be stopped”; speechlessness before God, general theme.

ezra-9:10:1.summary: Joshua's “What can I say” after Israel's failure echoes “What can we say, our God, after this?”

ezra-9:10:3.summary: Judah's “what shall we speak…God has found out the iniquity” parallels Esdras's speechless admission of guilt.

ezra-9:11:1.summary: Those “separating himself from the uncleanness of the nations of the land” matches the land's uncleanness in Esdras.
ezra-9:11:1.why: Same separation from the nations' uncleanness.

ezra-9:11:2.summary: The peoples of the lands “in their repulsive practices” use the same phrase as this verse.
ezra-9:11:2.why: Sets up the problem this prayer addresses.

ezra-9:11:3.summary: Nations' “abominations” for which the Lord destroys them reflect the prophetic warning Esdras cites.
ezra-9:11:3.why: Mosaic background to the cited warning.

ezra-9:11:4.summary: Cleansing “from all your uncleannesses”; general uncleanness theme.

ezra-9:11:5.summary: Nations' abominations, including child sacrifice; general theme of Canaanite practices.

ezra-9:11:6.summary: “Cleanse ourselves from every defilement”; general purity theme.

ezra-9:11:7.summary: Manasseh followed “the abominations of the nations”; general theme of nations' practices.
ezra-9:11:7.why: Example of adopting the nations' ways.

ezra-9:11:8.summary: Manasseh “filled Jerusalem from end to end” with blood; similar filling image, different sin.
ezra-9:11:8.why: Parallel image of a land filled with sin.

ezra-9:12:2.summary: Warning against those who “intermarry with them,” or perish “from this good land,” parallels Esdras's citation.

ezra-9:12:3.summary: “Take their daughters for your sons and give your daughters to their sons” closely matches Esdras's quotation.
ezra-9:12:3.why: Source law of the cited command.

ezra-9:12:4.summary: A good man leaves an inheritance to children's children; general inheritance theme.
ezra-9:12:4.why: Loose parallel of bequeathing to sons.

ezra-9:12:5.summary: Do not greet false teachers; general theme of separation.

ezra-9:12:6.summary: The blameless leaves his children blessed; general inheritance theme.

ezra-9:12:7.summary: The God-fearer's seed “will be powerful in the land”; loose parallel to becoming strong and bequeathing.

ezra-9:12:8.summary: Abraham will command his sons to keep the Lord's ways; general generational obedience theme.
ezra-9:12:8.why: Loose parallel of obedience for descendants.

ezra-9:12:9.summary: “You will eat the land's good things” matches “eat the good things of the land.”

ezra-9:12:10.summary: “Make no covenant with them”; general separation law, no marriage wording shown.

ezra-9:12:11.summary: They “have taken some of their daughters for themselves and their sons,” the very breach this command forbids.

ezra-9:12:12.summary: Commands kept by “your sons, and your sons' sons” in the land; general obedience-and-land theme.

ezra-9:12:13.summary: “Be strong” to keep the law and inherit the land; loose shared strength-and-land idea.
ezra-9:12:13.why: Loose parallel of strength through obedience.

ezra-9:12:14.summary: Jehoshaphat rebuked for befriending one hated by the Lord; general warning against alliances.

ezra-9:13:0.summary: God “has not…repaid us according to our lawless deeds,” matching “Thou hast lightened our lawless deeds.”
ezra-9:13:0.why: Same confession of punishment less than deserved.

ezra-9:13:2.summary: No complaint over one's sin; “let us return to the Lord”; general repentance theme.

ezra-9:13:3.summary: Saints Job says what came is “worthy of the sins,” lacking the less-than-deserved idea the link assumes.
ezra-9:13:3.why: Greek wording does not carry the link.

ezra-9:13:4.summary: Earlier lines of the same prayer on lawless deeds, captivity and God's leniency.

ezra-9:13:5.summary: God “changed His purpose according to His abundant mercy”; general mercy theme.
ezra-9:13:5.why: Loose parallel of mercy after sin.

ezra-9:13:6.summary: Plea about “all the hardship that has found us” parallels “everything that has come upon us.”

ezra-9:13:7.summary: God will judge “according to your ways” without mercy, contrasting Esdras's lightened punishment.
ezra-9:13:7.why: Contrast of full versus lightened judgment.

ezra-9:13:8.summary: “In wrath Thou wilt remember mercy”; general mercy-in-judgment theme.

ezra-9:13:9.summary: Paul's question about suffering in vain has no real tie to Esdras's confession.

ezra-9:14:0.summary: Israel “provoked the Lord…to destroy you,” matching “do not be provoked against us to the point of destruction.”
ezra-9:14:0.why: Recalls Horeb as precedent for wrath to destruction.

ezra-9:14:1.summary: “Let Me destroy them”; general divine threat of destruction.

ezra-9:14:2.summary: Taking “their daughters” as the holy seed mingles with “the peoples of the lands,” the same sin named here.

ezra-9:14:3.summary: “Should we remain in sin…?” loosely echoes returning to sin after grace.
ezra-9:14:3.why: Loose parallel of relapse after mercy.

ezra-9:14:4.summary: God threatens to consume the congregation “all at once”; general destruction theme.

ezra-9:14:5.summary: “I will consume them all at once”; general threat of destruction.

ezra-9:14:6.summary: “Sin no more, so that something worse may not happen”; general warning after deliverance.
ezra-9:14:6.why: Loose parallel of relapse after mercy.

ezra-9:14:7.summary: God's wrath to “destroy them” after the calf; general destruction theme.
ezra-9:14:7.why: Precedent of wrath against covenant breach.

ezra-9:14:8.summary: “Make no covenant with those dwelling in this land…Yet you did not obey”; general disobedience theme.

ezra-9:14:9.summary: Turning back after escaping defilements makes the last state worse; general relapse theme.
ezra-9:14:9.why: Loose parallel of returning to sin.

ezra-9:14:10.summary: God “certainly will not make you perish” but disciplines; general theme of discipline without annihilation.

ezra-9:14:11.summary: “Make no covenant with them”; general separation law.

ezra-9:14:12.summary: “Survivors of the sword…in your scattering”; shared survivor idea only.

ezra-9:14:13.summary: Nehemiah confronts Jews with foreign wives and makes them swear not to “give your daughters to their sons.”

ezra-9:14:14.summary: “If the Lord Sabaoth had not left us seed” matches the fear that “no remnant or survivor remains.”
ezra-9:14:14.why: Same idea of a God-preserved remnant.

ezra-9:14:15.summary: God would scatter them and end their memory but for the enemies; general near-destruction theme.

ezra-9:14:16.summary: Earlier in the prayer, God left “some of us for deliverance,” the remnant now feared lost.

ezra-9:15:0.summary: “If Thou dost closely watch lawless deeds…who will withstand?” matches “there is no standing before Thee.”
ezra-9:15:0.why: Same confession that none can stand.

ezra-9:15:1.summary: “You will die in your sins” is a different context; only incidental shared reference to sins.

ezra-9:15:2.summary: “You will die in your sin” shares only the generic idea of sin.

ezra-9:15:3.summary: The world made “answerable to God”; general guilt-before-God theme.

ezra-9:15:5.summary: “Thou art righteous in all that has come upon us…we have sinned” parallels Esdras's “Thou art righteous.”

ezra-9:15:6.summary: Joshua stands in filthy garments and his lawless deeds are removed; general guilt-and-cleansing theme.
ezra-9:15:6.why: Picture of standing guilty before God.

ezra-9:15:7.summary: “The Lord our God is righteous in everything” while “we did not listen” parallels Esdras's confession.

ezra-9:15:8.summary: “No one living will be justified before Thee” matches “no standing before Thee.”
ezra-9:15:8.why: Same confession of human guilt before God.

ezra-9:15:9.summary: “Our…lawless deeds are upon us”; general guilt theme.

ezra-9:15:11.summary: “How can a mortal be righteous before the Lord?”; general theme.
ezra-9:15:11.why: Loose parallel of no standing before God.

ezra-9:15:12.summary: Shares “Thou art righteous, Lord,” but Jeremiah goes on to complain, not confess.

ezra-9:15:13.summary: “All our righteousness is like a…rag…because of our lawless deeds”; general communal guilt.

ezra-9:15:15.summary: “Still in your sins” about the resurrection; only incidental shared reference to sins.

ezra-10:1:0.summary: Daniel, “confessing my sins and the sins of my people,” prays as Esdras prays and confesses for Israel.
ezra-10:1:0.why: Parallel exile-era confession for the people.

ezra-10:1:1.summary: The psalmist’s tears flow “since they did not keep Thy law,” like Esdras weeping over the people’s transgression.
ezra-10:1:1.why: Grief over others’ breaking of the law.

ezra-10:1:2.summary: Paul’s “great sorrow” for his people loosely parallels Esdras’s weeping over Israel.

ezra-10:1:3.summary: Solomon asks God to hear His people praying toward this house, loosely fitting Esdras praying before the house of God.

ezra-10:1:4.summary: “If we confess our sins” states generally the confession Esdras makes.

ezra-10:1:5.summary: Jesus weeping over the city is only generally akin to Esdras weeping for Israel.

ezra-10:1:6.summary: Daniel “prayed to the Lord God and confessed” with fasting, as Esdras prayed and confessed for the people.

ezra-10:1:7.summary: Esdras again stands before the people as “all the people were weeping” on hearing the law.
ezra-10:1:7.why: Another scene of Esdras and a weeping people.

ezra-10:1:8.summary: Zechariah’s national mourning loosely parallels the people’s weeping, without specific shared detail.

ezra-10:1:9.summary: God hearing Solomon’s prayer at the consecrated house loosely relates to praying before the house of God.

ezra-10:1:10.summary: The psalmist says “I will confess my lawlessness,” a general parallel to Esdras’s confession.

ezra-10:1:11.summary: Standing “before this house” to cry to God in distress loosely parallels Esdras praying before the house.
ezra-10:1:11.why: Crying to God at the temple.

ezra-10:1:12.summary: Leviticus foresees Israel confessing their and their fathers’ sins, generally fitting Esdras’s confession.

ezra-10:1:13.summary: Jeremiah weeping in secret over the Lord’s flock is a general parallel to weeping over Israel.

ezra-10:1:14.summary: Jeremiah longs to “weep day and night for this people,” loosely like Esdras’s weeping.

ezra-10:1:15.summary: Hosea’s call to return to the Lord with words of repentance loosely fits Esdras’s prayer.

ezra-10:1:16.summary: Joel calls the whole people, including children, to assemble while priests weep and plead, as a great weeping assembly gathers to Esdras.

ezra-10:1:17.summary: The people with “their wives, sons and daughters” join the covenant, loosely like the assembly of men, women and young men.

ezra-10:1:18.summary: Cornelius praying in his house has no specific connection to Esdras’s weeping confession.

ezra-10:1:19.summary: Gathering “the men, and the women, and the children” to hear the law loosely matches the mixed assembly around Esdras.

ezra-10:1:20.summary: All Judah standing before the Lord with children and women loosely parallels the assembly gathered to Esdras.

ezra-10:1:21.summary: Believers with wives and children praying on a beach share only incidental detail with Esdras’s assembly.

ezra-10:1:22.summary: At the Lord’s rebuke “the people raised their voice and wept,” as the people here “raised their weeping.”

ezra-10:2:0.summary: Nehemiah condemns “breaking faith with our God by establishing households with foreign wives,” the same sin Sechenias confesses.
ezra-10:2:0.why: Same problem recurring in Nehemiah’s day.

ezra-10:2:2.summary: The warning against covenant with the land’s inhabitants is the law behind the sin, though marriage is not named in the shown verse.

ezra-10:2:3.summary: “Only recognize your injustice” and God’s mercy loosely parallel Sechenias’s confession and hope.

ezra-10:2:4.summary: Confession bringing cleansing generally parallels Sechenias’s admission of sin with hope.

ezra-10:2:5.summary: James on favoritism as transgression has no specific link to foreign marriages.

ezra-10:2:6.summary: The list of offenders includes “the sons of Elam,” among them a “Iaiel,” matching Sechenias son of Iiel of the sons of Elam.
ezra-10:2:6.why: Shows Elam’s family among the offenders.

ezra-10:2:7.summary: The call for the ungodly to return and find abundant forgiveness loosely underlies Sechenias’s “patient hope.”

ezra-10:2:8.summary: God’s self-description as merciful and forgiving generally grounds the hope Sechenias expresses.
ezra-10:2:8.why: Character of God behind the hope.

ezra-10:2:9.summary: Samaia son of Sechenia, a gatekeeper, is not shown to be connected to Sechenias son of Iiel; only a name overlaps.

ezra-10:2:10.summary: “The sons of Ailam” in the census are the Elam clan to which Sechenias belongs, but the verse only gives a number.
ezra-10:2:10.why: Shows the family’s place among returnees.

ezra-10:2:11.summary: The census of “the sons of Ailam” records the Elam clan of Sechenias, adding only a number.
ezra-10:2:11.why: Shows the family’s place among returnees.

ezra-10:2:12.summary: “The sons of Elam-ar” may be a related Elam family, but the link to Sechenias’s clan is uncertain.

ezra-10:2:13.summary: “The men of Elam-aar” may be a related Elam family, but the link to Sechenias’s clan is uncertain.

ezra-10:3:1.summary: Those devoted to God’s word gather to Esdras over “the deported community’s covenant-breaking,” the crisis Sechenias now proposes to resolve.
ezra-10:3:1.why: Immediate background of the covenant proposal.

ezra-10:3:2.summary: Joshua warns that if Israel will “intermarry with them,” those nations become traps, the danger behind putting away foreign wives.

ezra-10:3:3.summary: Paul tells a believer not to “dismiss” an unbelieving wife who consents to stay, contrasting with putting away foreign wives.

ezra-10:3:4.summary: The psalmist’s fear of God’s judgments loosely relates to frightening the people “with the commandments.”
ezra-10:3:4.why: General theme of fearing God’s law.

ezra-10:3:5.summary: Leaders “establishing a pledge” and sealing it parallel making a covenant with God in general terms.

ezra-10:3:6.summary: Josiah fears God’s anger because the book’s words were not kept, loosely like acting “according to the law.”

ezra-10:3:7.summary: Entering “into the covenant of the Lord your God” parallels making a covenant with God only generally.

ezra-10:3:8.summary: Turning one’s feet toward God’s testimonies is too general to link specifically to the covenant to put away wives.

ezra-10:3:9.summary: Jehoiada’s covenant that the people be the Lord’s loosely parallels a leader-led covenant of reform.

ezra-10:3:10.summary: The Gibeonites asking Joshua for a covenant shares only the word “covenant” with Sechenias’s proposal.

ezra-10:3:11.summary: The people swear to keep God’s commandments and “not take their daughters for our sons,” a parallel covenant against intermarriage (truncated).

ezra-10:3:12.summary: The closing summary that “all these had taken foreign wives and had fathered sons” records the outcome of the proposed covenant.
ezra-10:3:12.why: Shows how the covenant was carried out.

ezra-10:3:13.summary: Those who “sigh deeply and grieve over all the lawlessness” loosely parallel the faithful responding to Israel’s sin.

ezra-10:3:14.summary: Hezekiah’s intent “to establish a covenant” to avert wrath resembles making a covenant with God, without the marriage issue.

ezra-10:3:15.summary: God regards one who “trembles at My words,” loosely like frightening the people with God’s commandments.

ezra-10:3:16.summary: Finding the booths law written in the book shares only general “written in the law” language with the covenant.

ezra-10:3:17.summary: God giving Judah one heart to keep the king’s ordinance shares nothing specific with the covenant to put away wives.

ezra-10:3:18.summary: Josiah establishes a covenant to keep God’s commandments as written in the book, loosely like doing all “according to the law.”

ezra-10:3:19.summary: Josiah humbling himself and weeping at God’s words loosely parallels the penitent response here.

ezra-10:3:20.summary: The Saints Isaiah 8:20 on law given “for help” has no specific link to the covenant to put away foreign wives.
ezra-10:3:20.why: Greek wording lacks a clear link.

ezra-10:3:21.summary: Upon hearing the law, “all the mixed population in Israel was separated,” a parallel reform acting on the written law.

ezra-10:4:0.summary: David’s charge to Solomon ends “Be strong and act,” the same words spoken to Esdras.
ezra-10:4:0.why: Same encouragement to undertake God’s work.

ezra-10:4:1.summary: “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your strength” is a general parallel to the call to act.

ezra-10:4:2.summary: Stirring one another to love and good works is too general to link to the charge to Esdras.

ezra-10:4:3.summary: David’s “Arise and build” resembles “Arise” here, but concerns building the sanctuary rather than reform.

ezra-10:4:4.summary: Strengthening drooping hands and weak knees is a general parallel to “Be strong.”

ezra-10:4:5.summary: Isaiah’s “Be strong; do not fear!” offers general encouragement like the charge to Esdras.

ezra-10:4:6.summary: David tells Solomon “Arise and act, and the Lord be with you,” closely matching “Arise… we are with you… act.”

ezra-10:4:7.summary: Artaxerxes’ letter gives Esdras authority to teach and enforce the law, background to “the matter rests upon you” (truncated).

ezra-10:4:8.summary: God tells Joshua “Arise!” to remove the sin among the people, loosely like Esdras urged to deal with covenant-breaking (truncated).

ezra-10:4:9.summary: The parable of a master assigning slaves work has no specific link to the charge to Esdras.

ezra-10:4:10.summary: David assures Solomon the priests, Levites and people “are with you in every undertaking,” as Esdras is told “we are with you.”
ezra-10:4:10.why: Community pledging support to a leader.

ezra-10:4:11.summary: The people pledge obedience to Joshua and end “Only be strong and courageous!”, much as they back Esdras with “Be strong and act.”
ezra-10:4:11.why: People pledging support to a leader.

ezra-10:5:1.summary: Nehemiah “made them swear to act according to this word,” virtually the same wording as Esdras’s oath.
ezra-10:5:1.why: Identical oath formula in a parallel reform.

ezra-10:5:0.summary: Nehemiah “made them swear by God” not to intermarry, a parallel oath on the same issue.

ezra-10:5:2.summary: The high priest adjuring Jesus shares only the idea of an oath with Esdras’s action.

ezra-10:5:3.summary: The proverb on a fitly spoken word has no specific link to Esdras making the leaders swear.

ezra-10:5:4.summary: The Saints Proverbs 15:23 speaks of the evil person not heeding, unrelated to the oath taken.

ezra-10:5:6.summary: The Saints Proverbs 27:9 on perfumes and misfortunes has nothing to do with the oath.

ezra-10:5:7.summary: Giving a wise person instruction is unrelated to Esdras making Israel swear.

ezra-10:5:8.summary: A wise person growing wiser by hearing is unrelated to the oath to act on this word.

ezra-10:5:9.summary: “This word” the people swear to is Sechenias’s proposal to make a covenant and put away the wives.

ezra-10:6:0.summary: Moses “ate no bread, and drank no water, because of all your sins,” as Esdras fasts mourning the people’s sin.

ezra-10:6:1.summary: Jesus’ food being to do God’s will is unrelated to Esdras’s mourning fast.

ezra-10:6:2.summary: Elisoub the high priest appears building the Sheep Gate; Ioanan is called son of Elisoub here.

ezra-10:6:3.summary: Nehemiah’s list names Joanan in the line of Eliasib, the priestly family behind “Ioanan son of Elisoub.”
ezra-10:6:3.why: Places Ioanan in the priestly line.

ezra-10:6:4.summary: Moses was before the Lord “eating no bread and drinking no water,” the same fast Esdras keeps.

ezra-10:6:5.summary: Elisoub the high priest, whose grandson married Sanaballat’s daughter, is the same Elisoub named as Ioanan’s father.

ezra-10:6:6.summary: “Bethelisoub of the high priest” refers to Elisoub’s house, giving only a passing link to the name.

ezra-10:6:7.summary: Job hiding God’s words in his breast has no specific link to Esdras’s fast.

ezra-10:6:8.summary: The high-priestly genealogy lists Eliasib, likely Elisoub, but adds only lineage.

ezra-10:6:10.summary: Daniel seeks God “with fasts, sackcloth, and ashes” over Israel’s sin, as Esdras fasts in mourning.

ezra-10:6:11.summary: The Lord calling for weeping and sackcloth loosely parallels Esdras’s mourning.

ezra-10:6:12.summary: Esdras’s weeping prayer “before the house of God” is the same scene from which he now arises.

ezra-10:6:13.summary: A large temple treasury chamber linked to Eliasib’s family is mentioned, loosely like Ioanan’s treasury chamber.
ezra-10:6:13.why: Temple chambers held by the priestly family.

ezra-10:7:0.summary: Cyrus “ordered a proclamation throughout his kingdom,” sharing only the proclamation motif.

ezra-10:7:1.summary: Hezekiah sends “a proclamation” throughout Israel inviting people to come to Jerusalem, as here.
ezra-10:7:1.why: Similar summons to assemble in Jerusalem.

ezra-10:8:1.summary: Being “put out of the synagogue” resembles being separated from the assembly, but in a different setting.

ezra-10:8:2.summary: The blind man “cast out” is a general parallel to separation from the assembly.
ezra-10:8:2.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

ezra-10:8:3.summary: The mixed population being “separated” shares the separation motif, though in a different sense.

ezra-10:8:4.summary: Saul’s summons threatens “whoever does not come out,” a parallel penalty on those who ignore a national call.

ezra-10:8:5.summary: The law of devoted things explains property “put under the ban,” but the shown verse concerns voluntary dedication.

ezra-10:8:6.summary: A great oath threatened anyone who “did not come up in the assembly,” paralleling the penalty for not arriving.

ezra-10:8:7.summary: “Remove the wicked person from among yourselves” is a general parallel to separation from the assembly.

ezra-10:8:8.summary: Being put out of the synagogues loosely parallels exclusion from the assembly.

ezra-10:8:9.summary: Treating the unrepentant as an outsider is a general parallel to separation from the assembly.

ezra-10:8:10.summary: Jericho’s metals made holy to the Lord’s treasury loosely relates to property put under the ban.

ezra-10:9:0.summary: Thunder and rain make the people fear at Samuel’s rebuke, loosely like the people trembling in winter weather.

ezra-10:9:2.summary: Esther’s audience in the twelfth month shares only a calendar date formula.

ezra-10:9:3.summary: God bringing rain from His treasuries has no specific link to the assembly in winter weather.

ezra-10:9:4.summary: The dates of Esdras’s arrival share only date formulas, not the event of the assembly.

ezra-10:10:0.summary: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” loosely parallels “adding to Israel’s offense.”

ezra-10:10:1.summary: Esdras’s earlier prayer says “our offenses have grown to heaven,” matching his charge of “adding to Israel’s offense.”
ezra-10:10:1.why: Same speaker on the same sin.

ezra-10:10:2.summary: Israel’s leaders refuse captives lest they bring sin “adding to our sins,” the same language of increasing guilt.
ezra-10:10:2.why: Same idea of adding to national sin.

ezra-10:10:3.summary: Moses accuses the tribes of rising up “to add still more to the fury of the Lord’s anger against Israel.”
ezra-10:10:3.why: Same charge of adding to Israel’s guilt.

ezra-10:10:4.summary: The sin of Peor bringing wrath on all Israel loosely parallels the communal guilt of foreign marriages.
ezra-10:10:4.why: Communal guilt from one group’s sin.

ezra-10:11:0.summary: Not conforming to this age and discerning what is “pleasing” loosely echoes doing what pleases God and separating.

ezra-10:11:1.summary: One who covers impiety will not prosper, generally fitting the call to confess.

ezra-10:11:2.summary: “Neither shall you intermarry with them,” lest they turn sons to other gods, is the law Esdras enforces.

ezra-10:11:3.summary: Joshua tells Achar “Give glory today to the Lord, the God of Israel, and make confession,” a parallel call to confess guilt.

ezra-10:11:5.summary: Leviticus foresees Israel confessing their sins and God remembering the covenant, a general parallel.

ezra-10:11:6.summary: “Wash yourselves… stop your evil deeds” is a general call to repentance like Esdras’s.

ezra-10:11:7.summary: Israel told to recognize injustice for spreading ways “to strangers” loosely fits the call to confess and separate.

ezra-10:11:8.summary: Confession bringing cleansing generally parallels Esdras’s call to give praise and repent.

ezra-10:11:9.summary: “Come out from their midst and be separated” echoes the command “Separate yourselves from the peoples.”

ezra-10:11:10.summary: Walking worthily and “pleasing Him in every way” loosely echoes doing what is pleasing before God.

ezra-10:11:11.summary: “I will confess my lawlessness… to the Lord” generally parallels the call to confession.

ezra-10:11:12.summary: Isaiah’s promise to eunuchs who keep the covenant shares only “choose what I wish” with doing God’s pleasure.

ezra-10:11:13.summary: On hearing the law “the mixed population in Israel was separated,” a parallel act of separation.

ezra-10:11:14.summary: The leaders report Israel “have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands,” the problem Esdras now addresses.

ezra-10:11:15.summary: Paul on receiving God’s Spirit rather than the world’s has no specific link to separating from foreign wives.

ezra-10:11:16.summary: God working “what is pleasing in His sight” loosely echoes doing what is pleasing before Him.

ezra-10:12:0.summary: Nehemiah sees Jews with foreign wives, the same problem, but the source verse is only the assembly’s reply.

ezra-10:12:1.summary: Israel’s unfaithful heart in the wilderness has no specific link to the assembly’s agreement.

ezra-10:12:2.summary: The assembly answers the proposal of verses 3–4 to make a covenant and “let it be done according to the law.”

ezra-10:12:3.summary: Israel breaking faith “like a crooked bow” has no specific link to the assembly’s agreement.
ezra-10:12:3.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

ezra-10:13:0.summary: The list of those with foreign wives shows the long work the people said was “not for one day or two” (truncated).
ezra-10:13:0.why: Shows the scale of the task.

ezra-10:13:1.summary: The narrow gate saying shares only the word “many” with the people’s practical objection.

ezra-10:14:0.summary: Hezekiah’s call promises God “will turn furious wrath away from you,” matching the aim to turn God’s wrathful anger away.

ezra-10:14:1.summary: Hezekiah establishes a covenant so “He will turn His furious wrath away from us,” as here.

ezra-10:14:2.summary: At Peor, action by the leaders makes “the Lord’s fierce anger… turn away from Israel,” a parallel case of wrath over foreign women.
ezra-10:14:2.why: Precedent for averting wrath over intermarriage.

ezra-10:14:3.summary: God turning back His wrath in compassion is a general parallel to averting His anger.

ezra-10:14:4.summary: God ceasing from anger after Achar’s sin is dealt with loosely parallels turning wrath away by removing the offense.
ezra-10:14:4.why: Wrath ended by dealing with sin.

ezra-10:14:5.summary: The king writing a copy of the law has no specific link to arranging the hearings for foreign marriages.

ezra-10:14:6.summary: Praise because God “didst turn Thy wrath away” loosely relates to the hope of averting wrath.

ezra-10:14:7.summary: Removing what is devoted so God turns “from the fierceness of His wrath” loosely parallels the plan here.

ezra-10:14:8.summary: Jehoshaphat appoints judges “city by city,” paralleling elders and judges of each city handling the cases.

ezra-10:14:9.summary: Bringing cases to priests and the judge loosely parallels judges involved in deciding these cases.

ezra-10:15:1.summary: A Mesoulam appears in the covenant list, but the shown text does not establish he is the same Mesoulam.

ezra-10:15:2.summary: Mesoulam son of Basodia repaired a gate, but nothing shows he is the Mesoulam who helped here.

ezra-10:15:3.summary: A Mesoulam walks with Esdras at the wall dedication, possibly but not demonstrably the same man.

ezra-10:16:0.summary: Job tracing out a case he did not know loosely parallels leaders sitting to examine the matter.

ezra-10:16:1.summary: The law to “inquire and search diligently” before acting loosely parallels examining the matter.

ezra-10:16:2.summary: Nicodemus’s point that the law first hears before judging loosely parallels examining each case.

ezra-10:18:0.summary: Both name “Iesous son of Iosedek”, the high priest whose sons are listed among those with foreign wives.
ezra-10:18:0.why: Identifies the high priestly family implicated in the marriages.

ezra-10:18:1.summary: Haggai addresses Joshua son of Jehozadak the high priest, the same figure as Iesous son of Iosedek.
ezra-10:18:1.why: Shows the stature of the family whose sons transgressed.

ezra-10:18:2.summary: Iesous appears as a leader returning with Zorobabel, the same high priest named in the source.
ezra-10:18:2.why: Places the high priest among the first returnees.

ezra-10:18:4.summary: Zechariah's vision features Joshua the high priest, the same Iesous son of Iosedek.
ezra-10:18:4.why: Links the family's sin to the high priest's accused, soiled standing.

ezra-10:18:5.summary: Law restricting whom priests may marry; it concerns prostitutes and divorced women, not foreign wives.

ezra-10:18:6.summary: Qualities of women in church office have no specific connection to priests' foreign marriages.

ezra-10:18:7.summary: This “Jesus” is a Levite teacher of the law, not Iesous son of Iosedek; only the name overlaps.

ezra-10:18:8.summary: Jeremiah condemns defiled priests; the source records priests who married foreign wives.

ezra-10:18:9.summary: The high priest must take a wife “from his own kin” and not “profane his seed”, the very rule the high priest's sons broke.
ezra-10:18:9.why: Supplies the law the priests violated.

ezra-10:18:10.summary: The leaders report that the priests had not separated from the peoples of the lands, the problem resolved in this list.
ezra-10:18:10.why: Opens the same episode that the list closes.

ezra-10:18:11.summary: Genealogy names Josadak, father of Iesous, deported to Babylon.
ezra-10:18:11.why: Traces the high priestly lineage of Iosedek.

ezra-10:18:12.summary: The high priestly line continues from Jesus (Iesous) through Joakim and Eliasib.
ezra-10:18:12.why: Shows the family line of the high priest named.

ezra-10:18:13.summary: A Maasaia stands beside Esdras at the reading, but nothing identifies him with the priest Maasea of the source.

ezra-10:18:14.summary: Malachi accuses priests of corrupting the covenant of Levi; the shown verses do not mention foreign marriage.

ezra-10:18:15.summary: Concerns adultery of Jerusalem's prophets, not priests' foreign wives; only a loose moral overlap.

ezra-10:18:16.summary: A son of the high priest's house became son-in-law of Sanaballat, another case of the high priestly family intermarrying with foreigners.
ezra-10:18:16.why: Shows the problem recurring in the same family.

ezra-10:18:17.summary: Eli's sons, priests, misbehave and are rebuked; parallel only as priests' sons doing wrong.
ezra-10:18:17.why: Loose analogy of errant priestly sons.

ezra-10:18:18.summary: Priests must marry “a virgin of Israel's offspring”, the standard broken by priests taking foreign wives.
ezra-10:18:18.why: States the priestly marriage rule directly.

ezra-10:19:0.summary: Both prescribe “a ram” from the flock for an “offence”, the guilt offering the priests brought.
ezra-10:19:0.why: Gives the law behind the priests' ram offering.

ezra-10:19:1.summary: “Give me your hand” as a gesture of pledge and loyalty, echoing “gave their hand in pledge”.

ezra-10:19:2.summary: The law of the “unblemished ram from the flock” “for his offence” matches the priests' guilt offering.
ezra-10:19:2.why: Explains the ram offered for offence.

ezra-10:19:3.summary: Saints text says the rulers “submitted”; no hand-giving or pledge wording carries the link.
